blocks.h: 1. What goal-based standards are, and the problem they solve

blocks.p: A prescriptive rule tells the builder what to do - this plate thickness, that scantling. It has two defects. It freezes the design practice of the year it was written, and it gives a designer no credit at all for a better idea that reaches the same safety by another route.

Goal-based standards invert that. The regulator states the outcome the ship must achieve, and for how long she must go on achieving it. Somebody else - the classification society, or the Administration through national standards - decides how. The regulator's job then becomes checking that the detailed rules genuinely deliver the stated outcome.

SOLAS regulation II-1/3-10 applies to oil tankers of 150 m in length and above and to bulk carriers of 150 m in length and above constructed with single deck, top-side tanks and hopper side tanks in cargo spaces, excluding ore carriers and combination carriers. It catches a ship by any one of three thresholds:

ul: building contract placed on or after 1 July 2016; or
in the absence of a contract, keel laid or similar stage of construction on or after 1 July 2017; or
delivery on or after 1 July 2020.

blocks.p: The standards themselves were adopted by resolution MSC.287(87) and made mandatory through this regulation. Naming the two ship types is worth a mark: they were chosen because bulk carriers and oil tankers dominated the serious structural-failure and pollution casualty record.

blocks.h: 3. The tier structure - and how many tiers the instrument contains

blocks.p: The framework is described in five tiers, but the adopted instrument contains only the top three. Getting this right separates a real answer from a memorised diagram:

rows: Tier I
The goals - what a safe and environmentally friendly ship is
IMO
Tier II
The functional requirements the ship must meet to achieve the goals
IMO
Tier III
Verification of conformity - how it is proved that Tier IV rules deliver Tiers I and II
IMO
Tier IV
The detailed class rules and national standards
Classification societies / Administrations
Tier V
Industry standards, codes of practice and quality systems
Industry

blocks.p: Tiers IV and V are not in the instrument. IMO deliberately did not write scantling rules; it wrote the goals and the machinery for checking somebody else's rules against them.

blocks.h: 4. Tier I and Tier II - the goal, and what it demands

blocks.p: The regulation states the goal directly: ships shall be designed and constructed for a specified design life to be safe and environmentally friendly, when properly operated and maintained under the specified operating and environmental conditions, in intact and specified damage conditions, throughout their life. It then defines the terms:

ul: Safe and environmentally friendly means adequate strength, integrity and stability to minimise the risk of loss of the ship, or of pollution, due to structural failure including collapse resulting in flooding or loss of watertight integrity.
Environmentally friendly also means the ship is constructed of materials for environmentally acceptable recycling.
Safety also includes structure, fittings and arrangements providing for safe access, escape, inspection and proper maintenance, and facilitating safe operation.

Specified operating and environmental conditions are defined by the intended operating area throughout the ship's life, including intermediate conditions from cargo and ballast operations in port, in waterways and at sea.

Specified design life is the nominal period the ship is assumed to be exposed to those conditions and to the corrosive environment - the period used to select design parameters. The actual service life may be longer or shorter.

blocks.p: Beneath the goal, Tier II sets fifteen functional requirements grouped by lifecycle phase - design, construction, in-service, and recycling. Two of their assumptions carry most of the engineering weight: a design life of not less than 25 years, and North Atlantic environmental conditions as the design environment regardless of the trade actually intended.

blocks.h: 5. Why this enhances safety and environmental protection

blocks.p: This is limb (a)'s real question and it should be answered as a set of consequences, not as praise.

ul: The goal is whole-life, not delivery-day. The words throughout their life and the 25-year design life force fatigue strength, corrosion additions and residual strength after damage into the design, rather than leaving them to be discovered in service.
Structural redundancy and residual strength become explicit objectives. A ship is required to survive specified damage, not merely to be strong when intact.

Accessibility and inspectability are written into the goal. A structure that cannot be reached cannot be surveyed, and a structure that is not surveyed fails quietly. This is the direct link to safe access and to the enhanced survey regime.

Corrosion control is pollution control. The dominant loss mechanism on both ship types is corrosion and fatigue leading to hull or tank breach; the goal that targets it protects the environment and the ship by the same measure.
Recycling is inside the goal, not bolted on. Requiring construction of materials for environmentally acceptable recycling reaches the end of the ship's life at the moment she is designed.
Transparency. The regime forces the design assumptions to be recorded and handed over, so that the people who maintain the ship know what she was designed to withstand.

blocks.h: 6. Tier III - how conformity is verified

blocks.p: This opens limb (b), and it is the part most candidates omit. The rules are audited, not self-certified.

ul: The regulation requires the goal to be achieved through the applicable structural requirements of an organization recognized by the Administration under regulation XI-1/1, or through national standards of the Administration, conforming to the functional requirements of the goal-based standards.

A classification society wishing its rules to be used submits them to IMO for verification of conformity, carried out under the Revised guidelines for verification of conformity, resolution MSC.454(100).
An audit team appointed by the Secretary-General, not the society itself, examines the rules against Tiers I and II and reports to the Maritime Safety Committee, which decides.
Verification is maintained, not granted once: when a society amends its rules the amendments are notified and the conformity has to be kept good.

rows: IMO
Owns Tiers I to III - sets the goals and the functional requirements, and runs the verification audits through MSC
Administration
Recognizes the organization under SOLAS XI-1/1, or writes national standards of equivalent safety, and enforces the regulation
Classification society
Writes the Tier IV rules, submits them for verification and maintains that conformity; approves plans; surveys during construction; assigns and maintains class
Ship designer
Designs to a verified rule set for the specified design life and environment, and delivers the design assumptions in a form somebody else can read
Shipbuilder
Delivers construction quality - materials, welding qualification, non-destructive testing, coatings - and compiles the Ship Construction File
Owner and operator
Maintains the ship so the design assumptions stay true, and keeps the File updated

blocks.p: The examiner's phrase various stakeholders is asking for exactly this division. The mark is for showing that each party's obligation is created by a different instrument - the society's by the verification guidelines, the Administration's by SOLAS XI-1/1, the builder's by the Ship Construction File requirement.

blocks.h: 8. The Ship Construction File - the part that survives delivery

blocks.p: SOLAS II-1/3-10 paragraph 4 requires that a Ship Construction File, with specific information on how the functional requirements of the goal-based standards have been applied in the design and construction, be provided upon delivery of a new ship, kept on board and/or ashore, and updated as appropriate throughout the ship's service. Its contents must at least conform to the guidelines developed by the Organization, at MSC.1/Circ.1343.

This is the mechanism that makes the whole regime operational rather than documentary. It carries the design life, the corrosion margins, the assumed loading conditions and the access arrangements forward to the people who will survey and repair the ship in twenty years - and it is the Chief Engineer's route to knowing what his ship was designed to withstand.

Eight marks each way, and the two limbs ask genuinely different things. Limb (a) is concept plus significance; limb (b) is process plus people. The commonest failure is to write one long essay on what goal-based standards are and then produce three lines on stakeholders, because the concept material is easier to recall. Steps 6, 7 and 8 are the whole of limb (b) and carry half the question.

The single highest-value discrimination on the page is knowing that the adopted instrument contains three tiers, not five. Tiers IV and V describe where class rules and industry practice sit in the framework; they are not part of what IMO adopted.

The regulator stopped writing the rules and started auditing them. Every other feature follows from that one move: the tiers exist because somebody has to say what the goal is and somebody else has to write the detail; the verification audit exists because the two are different people; the Ship Construction File exists because the design assumptions have to outlive the designer.

ul: Saying goal-based standards apply to all ships. They apply to bulk carriers and oil tankers of 150 m and above, with ore carriers and combination carriers excluded.

Giving the application date as the adoption date. The standards were adopted in 2010 and the regulation entered into force in 2012, but the requirement bites on a building contract on or after 1 July 2016.
Presenting five tiers as the content of the instrument.
Describing verification as the society certifying its own rules. It is an IMO audit reporting to MSC.
Omitting the Ship Construction File, or calling it a set of as-built drawings. It is a record of how the functional requirements were applied.
Answering limb (b) as a second description of the concept rather than as process and stakeholders.
'Which ships?' Bulk carriers and oil tankers, 150 m and above, single deck with top-side and hopper side tanks; ore carriers and combination carriers excluded.
'What design life?' Not less than 25 years, in North Atlantic environmental conditions - regardless of the intended trade.
'Who verifies the class rules?' An audit team appointed by the Secretary-General, reporting to MSC. Not the society, not the flag State.
'Is recycling part of a construction standard?' Yes - the goal requires construction of materials for environmentally acceptable recycling.
'Where does the Ship Construction File live?' Provided on delivery, kept on board and/or ashore, updated throughout service.
What is the difference between a prescriptive and a goal-based rule? Prescriptive states the means; goal-based states the outcome and audits the means somebody else chooses.
Why were bulk carriers and oil tankers chosen? They dominated the serious structural-failure and pollution casualty record.
What does the regulation actually require of the builder? Structural requirements of a recognized organization conforming to the functional requirements, plus delivery of the Ship Construction File.
What happens if a society changes its rules after verification? The conformity has to be maintained; amendments are notified and re-examined.

How does this relate to regulation II-1/3-1? II-1/3-1 requires every ship to be designed, constructed and maintained to recognized class rules; II-1/3-10 adds, for these two ship types, that those rules must themselves have been verified against goals set by IMO.

blocks.p: Concept, ships, tiers, goal, significance for limb (a). Verify, who, File for limb (b). If the tier table is written first it drives the rest of the answer, because every stakeholder in limb (b) is the owner of one tier.

blocks.h: Uncertainty, and the thirty-month reach back

blocks.p: This question shares a character-identical printed stem with a June 2026 sitting, thirty months later, and that answer was read in full and audited line by line before any structure was used. The audit found the subject unusually stable: every instrument this answer needs - the standards of 2010, the regulation in force since 2012, the 2016 contract threshold, the 2018 verification guidelines and the Ship Construction File circular - pre-dates this sitting by years, so nothing had to be reversed on substance. What was checked for and is absent: any 34th Assembly instrument, the Merchant Shipping Act 2025, and later work on extending goal-based standards to other ship types, which is an unfinished agenda item and is not law at this sitting or at any other. One citation was corrected rather than carried: the Ship Construction File sits at paragraph 4 of the regulation, not at paragraph 2.1. The tier count, the number of functional requirements, the 25-year design life and the North Atlantic assumption are the content of the adopted standards, which is not held in the corpus; they are declared as established instrument content and no provision has been invented to support them.

questions.understand_first: Rules used to tell a builder exactly what to do - how thick a plate, how big a scantling. That has two problems: it locks in the design practice of whenever it was written, and it gives no credit to a designer who reaches the same safety a better way. Goal-based standards turn it round. The regulator says what the ship must achieve and for how long she must keep achieving it, and leaves the detailed rule-writing to the people who have always done it - the classification societies. The regulator's job becomes checking that those detailed rules really do deliver the stated outcome. That is why the structure comes in layers: a plain statement of what a safe ship is at the top, the things she must functionally be able to do underneath it, and the detailed rule book below that - with an audit in between to join them up. And because the goal is about the whole of the ship's life rather than the day she is handed over, the assumptions behind the design have to be written down and handed over with her.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the goal-based standards question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 Concept against prescription. 2 Which ships and from when. 3 The tier structure. 4 The goal and the functional requirements. 5 Significance for safety and the environment. 6 How conformity is verified. 7 Who does what. 8 The Ship Construction File.
retrieval_cards.why: Eight marks each way; steps 6 to 8 are the whole of limb (b) and are the half most often squeezed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a goal-based standard, as distinct from a prescriptive rule?
retrieval_cards.answer: A prescriptive rule states the means - the thickness, the scantling. A goal-based standard states the outcome the ship must achieve and for how long, and leaves the detailed rules to a classification society or an Administration, whose rules are then audited against the goal.
retrieval_cards.why: The conceptual mark, and everything else follows from it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which ships does SOLAS II-1/3-10 apply to, and from when?
retrieval_cards.answer: Oil tankers of 150 m and above and bulk carriers of 150 m and above constructed with single deck, top-side tanks and hopper side tanks, excluding ore carriers and combination carriers. Caught by a building contract on or after 1 July 2016, or keel laid on or after 1 July 2017, or delivery on or after 1 July 2020.
retrieval_cards.why: The commonest factual error is applying it to all ships or giving the adoption date instead of the contract date.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How many tiers does the adopted instrument contain?
retrieval_cards.answer: Three. The framework is described in five tiers, but the adopted standards contain Tier I goals, Tier II functional requirements and Tier III verification of conformity. Tier IV is the classification society and national rules and Tier V is industry practice - neither is part of what IMO adopted.
retrieval_cards.why: The single highest-value discrimination on the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is a classification society's rule set verified as conforming?
retrieval_cards.answer: The society submits its rules to IMO under the Revised guidelines for verification of conformity, MSC.454(100). An audit team appointed by the Secretary-General examines them against Tiers I and II and reports to the Maritime Safety Committee, which decides. Verification is maintained when the rules are amended, not granted once.
retrieval_cards.why: Describing this as self-certification is a serious error; the audit is the whole point of Tier III.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is the Ship Construction File and what does the regulation require of it?
retrieval_cards.answer: A file with specific information on how the functional requirements of the goal-based standards have been applied in the ship's design and construction. Paragraph 4 requires it to be provided on delivery of a new ship, kept on board and/or ashore, and updated as appropriate throughout the ship's service, with contents at least conforming to MSC.1/Circ.1343.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the mechanism that carries the design assumptions to the people who will survey and repair the ship decades later.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do regulations II-1/3-1 and II-1/3-10 differ?
retrieval_cards.answer: II-1/3-1 requires every ship to be designed, constructed and maintained to the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a recognized classification society, or equivalent national standards. II-1/3-10 adds, for bulk carriers and oil tankers of 150 m and above, that those rules must themselves have been verified as conforming to goals set by IMO.
retrieval_cards.why: One points at the rule book; the other audits it. Confusing them loses the point of goal-based standards.

blocks.h: 1. What port State control is - and what it is not

ul: The inspection of foreign ships in national ports to verify that the condition of the ship and her equipment, the competence and certification of her crew, and the manner in which she is operated, comply with the requirements of the international conventions.

It is a safety net beneath the flag State, not a substitute for it. It does not transfer the flag State's responsibility; the flag State remains the primary regulator and is notified of what is found.
It operates in practice through regional memoranda of understanding, which coordinate targeting, share inspection data and avoid the same ship being inspected repeatedly in one region.
It is not a survey, and not a commercial vetting inspection. Its purpose is to identify a substandard ship and to see her corrected.

blocks.h: 2. The legal framework - where the power actually comes from

blocks.p: This is the heart of limb (a) and the mark is for knowing that the power is conferred by the conventions themselves, each of which contains its own control article. The IMO procedures are guidance on how to exercise that power; they do not create it.

blocks.p: Above these sits UNCLOS article 218 and articles 219 and 226, which recognise the port State's enforcement jurisdiction and require that a ship not be unreasonably detained. And beneath them sits the flag State's own primary duty under UNCLOS article 94, which is what port State control is a net beneath.

blocks.h: 3. The IMO procedures, and the regional layer

blocks.p: IMO publishes a consolidated set of Procedures for Port State Control, revised periodically by the Assembly. At this sitting the edition in circulation is the one adopted by the 32nd Assembly in 2021. The 33rd Assembly adopted a 2023 revision on 6 December 2023 - within the month of this examination; this paper prints no day and no claim is made about which side of that date it fell. Nothing in this answer depends on the point, for a reason worth stating in the exam:

ul: The Procedures are recommendatory. The resolution adopts them and invites Governments to implement them. It confers no power and removes none - the power is in the conventions above.
The structure the question asks about is unchanged across the two editions: initial inspection, clear grounds, more detailed inspection, detention, notification to the flag State.

blocks.p: The operational layer is regional. Port States coordinate through memoranda of understanding - Paris, Tokyo, Indian Ocean, Mediterranean, Black Sea, Caribbean, Vina del Mar, Abuja and Riyadh. India is a member of the Indian Ocean MOU, and inspections in Indian ports are carried out by surveyors of DG Shipping under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and the rules made under it.

A short paragraph that earns its marks. The conventions provide that ships of States which are not Parties, and ships below convention size, shall be given no more favourable treatment than ships entitled to fly the flag of a Party. The effect is that not ratifying buys no advantage, which is what makes the whole system workable.

blocks.h: 5. How an inspection becomes a detention

ul: Initial inspection - the certificates and documents are examined and the officer forms a general impression of condition, including engine room and accommodation.

Clear grounds - evidence that the ship, her equipment or her crew does not correspond substantially with the certificates, or that the crew is unfamiliar with essential shipboard procedures. This is the legal trigger, and it must exist before the inspection goes further.
More detailed inspection - directed at the areas where the clear grounds arose.
Detention - where deficiencies are clearly hazardous to safety, health or the environment, the ship is detained until they are rectified or until she may proceed without unreasonable danger.
Notification - the detention is reported to the flag State in sufficient detail for the severity to be assessed, and to the recognized organization that issued the certificates.

Proceeding to a repair port - where the deficiency cannot be remedied at the port of inspection, the officer may allow the ship to proceed to another port on conditions, notifying the next port and the flag State.

blocks.h: 6. The right of appeal - what it is, and what it does not do

blocks.p: This opens limb (b), and three points carry it.

ul: The right is the Company's, not the Chief Engineer's. The Procedures state that the company or its representative have a right of appeal against a detention taken by the authority of a port State. The Chief Engineer, as such, does not hold it - which is the discrimination the printed question is actually testing.
The appeal does not suspend the detention. The ship stays detained while the appeal is heard. Arguing is not a way to sail.
The officer must inform the master of the right of appeal.

blocks.p: The appeal is then pursued at two levels in practice: to the port State authority itself under its national administrative procedure, and through the regional MOU's review mechanism, which can have a detention recorded as unjustified and removed from the ship's and the company's record. The flag State is the company's most effective ally: it may take the matter up with the port State directly, and where the certificates were issued by a recognized organization that organization is drawn in too.

blocks.h: 7. What the Chief Engineer should actually do

blocks.p: The question addresses the Chief Engineer directly, so the answer must separate his job from the Company's.

ul: Record the evidence before anything is changed. Photographs, readings, alarm and event logs, planned maintenance records, the certificates as presented. Once the defect is rectified the evidence that it was not hazardous is gone.
Ask, politely and in writing, which requirement each deficiency rests on. A deficiency has to be traceable to a provision. This is the single most useful thing he can do, and it is not an argument.
Notify immediately - master, Company and Designated Person, flag State Administration, and the recognized organization that issued the certificate.

Rectify and contest in parallel, never in sequence. Getting the ship to sea is an engineering job; challenging the detention is a legal one belonging to the Company. Doing the second instead of the first keeps the ship alongside.
Keep it professional. The officer is exercising a treaty power. The record made in the first hour is what the Company's appeal will be built on.

blocks.h: 8. Undue delay and compensation - a different remedy

blocks.p: Where a ship is unduly detained or delayed, the conventions provide a remedy in damages: MARPOL article 7(2) and the corresponding provisions of SOLAS regulation I/19 and LOAD LINES article 21 require that every effort be made to avoid undue detention, and entitle the ship to compensation for loss or damage suffered.

Two traps live here. First, compensation is a claim, not a release - it is pursued afterwards and does nothing to get the ship to sea. Second, it is a different remedy from the appeal: the appeal attacks the detention, the compensation claim attacks the loss it caused, and they are pursued in different places. A candidate who runs them together loses the discrimination the limb is testing.

Eight and eight, and the two limbs are entirely different tasks. Limb (a) is a legal-framework question - it says so - and it wants convention articles, not a description of an inspection. Limb (b) is an applied question addressed to you personally, and its marks are in the distinction between what the Company may do and what you should do.

The commonest way to lose limb (a) is to write a good description of how a port State control inspection is conducted. That is not what was asked. Name the instruments and their control articles - that is the framework.

Two separate things are happening and mixing them is what costs marks. Getting the ship to sea is engineering and procedure: fix the defect, satisfy the officer, have the detention lifted. Arguing that the detention was wrong is legal, belongs to the Company rather than to you, and changes nothing about tomorrow's sailing - the instrument says in one line that the appeal does not suspend the detention.

ul: Answering limb (a) with inspection procedure instead of legal authority.
Saying the power comes from the IMO procedures. It comes from the conventions; the procedures are guidance and say themselves that Governments are invited to implement them.
Claiming the Chief Engineer has a personal right of appeal. The company or its representative holds it.
Saying the appeal suspends the detention. It does not.
Treating a regional memorandum of understanding as a treaty. It is an administrative agreement between authorities.
Forgetting no more favourable treatment, which is a cheap and reliable mark.
Confusing the appeal with the compensation claim for undue delay.
'Under what authority does a port State inspect your ship?' The control article of each convention - SOLAS I/19, MARPOL 5 and 6, LOAD LINES 21, STCW X, and so on.
'You think the detention is unfair. Can you appeal?' Not personally. The Company or its representative appeals; you gather and preserve the evidence.
'Will the appeal get you to sea?' No. It does not suspend the detention.
'The ship is registered in a State that is not a Party. Better or worse for you?' Neither - no more favourable treatment.
'What must exist before a detailed inspection?' Clear grounds.
'Who is told about the detention?' The flag State, in sufficient detail to assess severity, and the organization that issued the certificates.
What are clear grounds? Evidence that the ship, equipment or crew does not correspond substantially with the certificates, or that the crew is unfamiliar with essential shipboard procedures.
Which regional arrangement covers Indian ports? The Indian Ocean MOU; inspections are by DG Shipping surveyors under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958.
Can the ship sail to a repair port? Yes, at the officer's discretion and on conditions, with the next port and the flag State notified.
What can you claim if the detention was undue? Compensation for loss or damage under the convention provisions on undue delay - but it is a claim after the event, not a release.
Who is ultimately responsible for the ship's compliance? The flag State. Port State control is a net beneath it and does not transfer that duty.

blocks.p: Limb (a): what it is, where the power is, the region, no more favourable treatment, how it becomes a detention. Limb (b): who holds the right, what it does not do, what you do, and the separate compensation remedy. If the convention table is written first, limb (a) is already half answered.

blocks.h: Uncertainty - the boundary this question sits on

blocks.p: This is one of two questions on the paper that sit on a real boundary. IMO's consolidated Procedures for Port State Control were revised by the Assembly during the very month of this examination, and the paper prints no day, so it is not possible to say whether the sitting fell before or after that revision was adopted. The answer is deliberately written so that it does not matter. Both editions were examined; the revision adopts the new Procedures, invites Governments to implement them and revokes its predecessor, with no deferred-effect clause and, importantly, no change to the inspection and detention structure this question asks about. Because the Procedures only invite implementation they are recommendatory and confer no legal power at all - the power is in the conventions, and no convention moved in December 2023. The later revision's own text, in any event, was not published as a document until January of the following year. A candidate answering from either edition gives the same answer, and this one names neither as the source of the legal power.

questions.understand_first: Two different things are going on in this question and mixing them is what loses the marks. The first is a question about authority: a port State is stopping and inspecting a ship that belongs to somebody else's register, and the mark is for knowing that it is allowed to do that because each of the great conventions contains its own clause saying so. The published inspection manual is guidance on how to use that power; it is not the source of it. The second is practical and personal. If the ship is held and you think the reasons are unfair, there are two separate jobs and they are not yours to combine. Getting the ship to sea is engineering: put the defect right, satisfy the officer, have the ship released. Arguing that holding her was wrong is legal, it belongs to the company rather than to you, and it will not move tomorrow's sailing by an hour - the manual says in one line that appealing does not lift the detention. What you can do, and what matters most, is preserve the evidence before you repair anything, because once the defect is fixed the proof that it was never dangerous has gone.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are clear grounds, and what do they trigger?
retrieval_cards.answer: Evidence that the ship, her equipment or her crew does not correspond substantially with the certificates, or that the crew is unfamiliar with essential shipboard procedures. They are the legal trigger for a more detailed inspection and must exist before one is carried out.

retrieval_cards.prompt: As Chief Engineer, can you appeal against a detention you think is unfair?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not personally. The company or its representative has the right of appeal. The appeal does not cause the detention to be suspended, and the officer should properly inform the master of the right. Your job is to preserve the evidence, establish which requirement each deficiency rests on, notify the company, flag State and the recognized organization, and rectify while the company contests.
retrieval_cards.why: The printed limb invites the confusion; the discrimination is where the marks are.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the compensation remedy differ from the appeal?
retrieval_cards.answer: The appeal attacks the detention itself and is pursued with the port State authority and through the regional review mechanism. Compensation for undue delay, under MARPOL article 7(2) and the corresponding SOLAS and Load Lines provisions, attacks the loss the detention caused and is claimed afterwards. It is not a route to release.
retrieval_cards.why: Running the two together loses the discrimination the limb tests.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the no-more-favourable-treatment principle.
retrieval_cards.answer: Ships of States that are not Parties to a convention, and ships below convention size, are given no more favourable treatment than ships entitled to fly the flag of a Party. Not ratifying therefore buys no advantage.

blocks.h: 1. The types of loss in marine insurance

blocks.p: Losses divide first into total and partial. Two further heads - salvage charges and particular charges - are recoverable but are not, strictly, losses of the subject matter, and saying so is worth a mark.

rows: Total loss
Actual total loss

The subject matter is destroyed, or so damaged that it ceases to be a thing of the kind insured, or the assured is irretrievably deprived of it. A missing ship is treated as an actual total loss after a reasonable time
Total loss
Constructive total loss

The subject matter is reasonably abandoned because actual total loss appears unavoidable, or because it could not be preserved or repaired without expenditure exceeding its value when repaired. It requires a notice of abandonment, without which the loss is treated as partial
Partial loss
Particular average
Accidental, fortuitous damage to one interest, borne by that interest alone. Nobody contributes
Partial loss
General average
A deliberate, extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure for the common safety, shared rateably by all the interests saved
Charges
Salvage charges
Charges recoverable by a salvor independently of contract, for services rendered in saving the property from peril
Charges
Particular charges - sue and labour
Expenses incurred by or for the assured to avert or minimise a loss, other than general average and salvage charges. Recoverable in addition to a total loss

blocks.p: The pivot of the whole classification is deliberateness. Particular average is what the sea did to you; general average is what you chose to do about it.

blocks.h: 2. The general average act, as the 1994 Rules define it

blocks.p: The examiner has named the York-Antwerp Rules 1994, and Rule A is where the definition lives. In substance it provides that there is a general average act when, and only when, any extraordinary sacrifice or expenditure is intentionally and reasonably made or incurred for the common safety, for the purpose of preserving from peril the property involved in a common maritime adventure; and that general average sacrifices and expenditures are borne by the several contributing interests on the basis set out in the Rules.
Five words in that sentence each carry a condition, and the next step unpacks them. The wording of Rule A is unchanged in the 2016 edition, so a candidate who learns it once has it for either.

blocks.h: 3. The circumstances in which general average can be declared

blocks.p: Set these out as separate conditions - the examiner is counting them.

ul: There must be a real peril, present and substantial, threatening the common adventure. Apprehension of a danger that has not arisen is not enough.
The act must be extraordinary. Doing what the ship is contractually bound to do, or what ordinary good seamanship requires, is not a general average act however expensive it proves.
It must be intentional and voluntary - a decision, not an accident. Cargo swept overboard by the sea is particular average; cargo jettisoned to lighten the ship is general average.
It must be reasonable. The Rule Paramount - in these terms in the 1994 edition - provides that no allowance shall be made unless the sacrifice or expenditure was reasonably made or incurred.
It must be for the common safety, that is for the benefit of the whole adventure and not of one interest alone. Sacrificing cargo to save only the ship is not general average.
There must be a common maritime adventure - at least two interests at risk, typically ship, cargo and freight.
Property must in fact be saved. There must be a fund to contribute; if everything is lost there is nothing to share.

The declaration is made by the shipowner, through the Master, who appoints an average adjuster; general average security - a general average bond from cargo interests and a general average guarantee from their underwriters - is taken before cargo is released.

blocks.p: Classic examples: jettison of cargo; voluntary stranding to prevent foundering; damage from extinguishing a fire aboard, including water damage to sound cargo; engine damage caused deliberately in working a stranded ship off; and port of refuge expenses - putting in, discharging to effect repairs, and the associated wages and maintenance.

blocks.h: 4. Why the 1994 edition matters, since the examiner named it

ul: The Rules are contractual, not law. They bind only because the contract of carriage and the policy incorporate them, and the edition is whichever the contract names. That is the first mark in this step.
Rule XX (1994) allows a commission of 2 per cent on general average disbursements other than crew wages and maintenance and fuel and stores not replaced.

Rule XXI (1994) allows interest at 7 per cent per annum on expenditure, sacrifices and allowances until three months after the adjustment is issued. Later editions replaced that fixed rate with an annually determined one.
The 1994 Rules end at Rule XXII and contain no time bar. A time-bar rule appears only in later editions.
The 2016 edition is the newer text a modern contract may incorporate. It is not a superseding law and it does not amend the 1994 Rules; if the contract says 1994, the 1994 Rules apply.

blocks.h: 5. Warranties in marine insurance - and what breach does

blocks.p: Limb (b) turns on a word that means something different here than in ordinary contract law. In ordinary contract law a warranty is the minor term. In marine insurance it is the severe one.

ul: A marine-insurance warranty is a promissory warranty: the assured undertakes that some thing shall or shall not be done, that some condition shall be fulfilled, or affirms or negatives the existence of a particular state of facts.
It must be exactly complied with, whether it is material to the risk or not. Substantial compliance is not compliance.

Under the Indian Act, as under the English Act of 1906 on which it is modelled, breach discharges the insurer from liability as from the date of the breach. It does not avoid the policy from inception, and the insurer remains liable for anything that happened before.

Breach is excused only narrowly - where circumstances change so the warranty ceases to be applicable, or where compliance is made unlawful by a subsequent law. A remedy of the breach before loss does not, of itself, restore cover under this rule.

The English Insurance Act 2015 changed the English position, converting breach into a suspension of liability that revives on remedy, and preventing an insurer relying on a breach irrelevant to the loss. That is English law. It is not the Indian rule, and saying so is a high-value discrimination.

blocks.h: 6. Express warranties, with a hull and machinery example

ul: An express warranty is one written into or upon the policy, or contained in a document incorporated into it by reference. No particular form of words is required - what matters is that the intention to warrant is clear.
It does not exclude an implied warranty unless it is inconsistent with it.

blocks.p: Hull and machinery examples, any one of which answers the question:

ul: Classification warranty - warranted classed and class maintained with a named or approved society, with the assured undertaking to report to underwriters any change, suspension, withdrawal or expiry of class. This is the commonest and best example, and it links directly to the classification regime.
Navigation and trading limits - warranted no Baltic winter trading, or trading confined to defined institute limits.
Lay-up warranty - a return of premium warranted only for a laid-up and out-of-commission period in a safe port.
Warranted no towage or salvage services, save as customary or under standard terms.

blocks.h: 7. Implied warranties, and the twist that catches candidates

ul: An implied warranty is imposed by law and is in the policy without being written in it.
Legality of the adventure - a warranty that the adventure is lawful and, so far as the assured can control it, will be carried out lawfully. This one cannot be excluded by agreement.

Seaworthiness in a voyage policy - a warranty that the ship shall be seaworthy at the commencement of the voyage for the purpose of that particular adventure, including being properly manned, equipped, fuelled and supplied.

Here is the twist that decides the mark in a hull and machinery question: there is NO implied warranty of seaworthiness in a TIME policy, and a hull and machinery policy is normally written for a period of time. There is also no implied warranty as to the nationality of the ship.

blocks.p: But unseaworthiness is not irrelevant to a time policy. Where, with the privity of the assured, the ship is sent to sea in an unseaworthy state, the insurer is not liable for any loss attributable to that unseaworthiness. That is a narrower and different rule from a warranty: it requires the owner's knowledge or blind-eye awareness, and it defeats only the loss the unseaworthiness caused - not the whole policy.

The contract - written in the policy or a document incorporated by reference
The law - present without being written
Can it be excluded?
It is the parties' own term; they choose it
Legality cannot be excluded; others may be excluded by clear words

Warranted classed and class maintained; trading limits; lay-up warranty
Legality of the adventure. Seaworthiness applies only to a voyage policy - not to a time policy

Insurer discharged from liability from the date of breach, materiality irrelevant

blocks.p: Limb (a) prints as one limb but is three separate questions - types of loss, the definition, and the circumstances - for eight marks between them. The route gives each a step so none is squeezed. Limb (b) is a single clean comparison and should be finished with the small table, which earns more than another paragraph of prose.

The distinguishing move in limb (a) is step 4. The examiner has named the 1994 edition, and a candidate who explains that the Rules are contractual and that the named edition is what applies has shown he understands what the Rules are, not merely what they say.

Two ideas, and both are counter-intuitive. First, general average is not compensation for damage - it is the sharing out of a loss somebody chose to suffer on purpose to save the whole venture, which is why everyone who benefited pays a share. Second, in marine insurance a warranty is the severe term, not the minor one: it must be kept exactly, whether or not it has anything to do with the loss, and breaking it ends the insurer's liability from that moment.

ul: Confusing particular average with general average. Particular average is accidental and borne alone; general average is deliberate and shared.
Omitting the notice of abandonment from constructive total loss. Without it the loss is treated as partial.
Reciting Rule A without unpacking the conditions. The circumstances are a separate task and are separately marked.
Saying the York Antwerp Rules are law. They are contractual and bind by incorporation.
Answering to the 2016 edition when the question names 1994.
Saying breach of warranty avoids the policy from inception. It discharges the insurer from the date of breach.
Stating an implied warranty of seaworthiness in a hull and machinery time policy. There is none - the classic error on this limb.
Applying the English 2015 reform as though it were the Indian rule.
'Cargo washed overboard in heavy weather - general average?' No. Accidental, therefore particular average.
'Cargo jettisoned to lighten a grounded ship?' Yes - deliberate, extraordinary, for the common safety.
'Nothing was saved. Can general average be declared?' No. There must be a contributing fund.

'Your hull policy is a time policy. Is there an implied warranty of seaworthiness?' No - but if the ship went to sea unseaworthy with the owner's privity, a loss attributable to that unseaworthiness is not covered.

'You breached a warranty but fixed it before the casualty. Are you covered?' Under the Indian rule, no - remedy before loss does not restore cover. Under the English Act of 2015 it would. Say which system you are answering in.
'Which edition of the Rules applies to your voyage?' Whichever the contract of carriage and the policy name.

What is a notice of abandonment and when is it given? Notice to the underwriter that the assured abandons the subject matter, given with reasonable diligence once he has reliable information of a constructive total loss.

What security is taken before cargo is released in general average? A general average bond from cargo interests and a general average guarantee from their underwriters, with a deposit as an alternative.
Who declares general average and who adjusts it? The shipowner declares, through the Master; an average adjuster prepares the statement.
Give three port-of-refuge items allowable in general average. Cost of putting in, discharging to effect repairs, and wages and maintenance during the detention.
Name the express warranty you would expect in every hull policy. Warranted classed and class maintained, with an obligation to report change, suspension or withdrawal of class.

For the conditions use peril, extraordinary, intentional, reasonable, common, adventure, saved - seven words, seven marks-bearing propositions. Limb (b): severe not minor, then express, then implied - and the time-policy twist last, because it is the highest-value point on the limb.

questions.understand_first: Two ideas sit under this question and both run against the ordinary meaning of the words. The first is that general average is not compensation for damage at all. It is the sharing out of a loss that somebody chose to suffer on purpose - throwing cargo over the side, deliberately running a sinking ship aground, flooding a hold to put out a fire - because doing so saved the whole venture. Everyone whose property was saved therefore pays a share. That single idea separates it from ordinary damage, which the sea inflicts on you and which you bear alone. The second is that a warranty here is not the small print. In ordinary contracts a warranty is the minor promise and breaking it earns damages. In marine insurance it is the severe one: it has to be kept exactly, whether or not it had anything to do with what went wrong, and breaking it ends the insurer's liability from that moment onward. Notice also that some of these promises are written into the policy and some are put there by law whether anyone writes them or not - and the ones the law implies do not all apply to every kind of policy.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the conditions for declaring general average.
retrieval_cards.answer: A real and present peril; an extraordinary act, not ordinary seamanship or a contractual duty; intentional and voluntary; reasonable, under the Rule Paramount; for the common safety rather than one interest; a common maritime adventure with at least two interests at risk; and property actually saved so there is a fund to contribute. retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish express from implied warranties and give a hull and machinery example of each.
retrieval_cards.answer: An express warranty is written into or upon the policy, or in a document incorporated by reference, in no particular form of words - for example 'warranted classed and class maintained', or trading limits, or a lay-up warranty. retrieval_cards.prompt: Is seaworthiness implied in a hull and machinery policy?
retrieval_cards.answer: No, because a hull and machinery policy is normally a time policy and there is no implied warranty of seaworthiness in a time policy. blocks.h: 1. Why decarbonisation changes what an engineer must be competent at

blocks.p: The important claim is not that engineers must work harder at what they already know. It is that the hazard has changed in kind. Heavy fuel oil hurt you by burning. The fuels now arriving hurt you in ways the existing training does not reach:

ul: one is poisonous well before it is flammable;
one burns with a flame you cannot see in daylight;
one escapes through joints that would hold oil, and embrittles the steel it escapes through;
one stores its energy chemically, so you cannot make it safe by shutting a valve.

blocks.p: A competence framework built around a hot, oily, flammable liquid does not transfer to any of those by degrees. That is the case for upskilling, and it should be the opening sentence of the answer.

blocks.h: 2. The driver, as it stands at this sitting

ul: The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy was adopted at MEPC 80 on 7 July 2023, replacing the Initial Strategy of 2018. It sets the trajectory - uptake of zero or near-zero GHG emission technologies, fuels and energy sources, with indicative checkpoints on the way. It is policy, not law, and saying so is a mark.

What is law, and already running: EEXI and the operational carbon intensity indicator under MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4 have applied since 1 January 2023. 2023 is the first CII data year, so the first ratings will not be assigned until 2024 - the regime is being implemented at this sitting, not yet mature.
No market-based measure has been adopted. There is no IMO carbon price and no fuel levy. The candidate who says otherwise is describing a debate, not an instrument.
The strategy's effect on manpower is direct: a fleet that must change fuel needs engineers who can run the new plant, and the ships are ordered years before the training framework catches up.

blocks.h: 3. Where the mandatory training framework reaches - and where it does not

blocks.p: This is the sharpest point available on limb (a) and few candidates make it.

ul: STCW regulation V/3 and section A-V/3 set mandatory minimum training, at basic and advanced level, for seafarers on ships subject to the IGF Code. That is the framework, and it works.

The IGF Code was built around gas and other low-flashpoint fuels, with LNG as the worked case. Ships burning methanol operate under interim guidelines rather than a matured Code chapter, and ammonia and hydrogen have no adopted IMO safety guidelines at all at this date - the work is under development.

The consequence: the training obligation is thinnest exactly where the hazard is newest. Competence for ammonia and hydrogen is being supplied by makers, owners and training providers, not by the Convention.
A comprehensive review of STCW is under way but has produced nothing yet. It is the right long-term route and it will not arrive in time for the ships already on order.

The practical answer at this sitting is therefore company-led: fuel-specific familiarisation beyond the Convention minimum, maker training, simulator work, and a risk assessment done by the ship's own staff.

blocks.h: 4. The anticipated areas of concern - fuel by fuel

headers: What the engineer must newly be competent at
rows: Ammonia

Acute toxicity is the governing hazard, not fire. Detection at very low concentration, escape sets and full protective equipment, water-based mitigation, venting and purge philosophy, absolute segregation from accommodation intakes. And the honest point: ammonia is not zero-emission - unburnt slip and nitrous oxide production must be managed
Methanol

Low flashpoint, and a flame that is nearly invisible in daylight. Alcohol-resistant foam, not conventional foam. Toxicity by ingestion and absorption. Double-walled piping, inerting and leak detection
Hydrogen

Extremely wide flammability range and very low ignition energy. Leakage through joints that would hold oil, and hydrogen embrittlement of materials. Cryogenic storage or very high pressure, and detection of a colourless, odourless gas
Batteries and hybrid systems

Stored energy that cannot be isolated by shutting a valve. Thermal runaway and its fire-fighting implications, high-voltage safety and permit systems, state-of-charge management and ventilation of battery spaces
LNG
The maturest of them, and already inside the Code. Cryogenic burns and material embrittlement, boil-off management, rollover, and gas-mode changeover
Biofuels and blends
Stability and compatibility, microbial growth, cold-flow properties, and the effect on fuel-system materials and lubricating oil selection
Wind assistance and shore power
Rotor and rig operation and its effect on stability and the loading condition; high-voltage shore connection procedures and synchronisation

blocks.h: 5. The competences that are not about fuel at all

ul: Efficiency operation and data integrity. The CII regime turns operational data into a compliance outcome. The engineer must understand what he is reporting and why an error in it is now a compliance failure and not just a bad number.
Dual-fuel changeover at sea, and the judgement of when not to attempt it.
Risk assessment for a plant nobody has operated for twenty years. Where there is no accumulated fleet experience, the ship's own hazard identification is the control.
Emergency response written for the new hazard - a toxic release drill is not a fire drill.
Leadership and change management, because the crew has to be brought through a change of fuel without losing the safety culture built around the old one.

blocks.h: 6. Why communication is a causal factor, not a contributory nicety

blocks.p: Limb (b) opens with the word the examiner used. Causal means it is a link in the chain, not a regrettable feature of the background.

The recurring pattern in casualty investigation is that the information existed on board and did not arrive where the decision was taken. Somebody knew the pump had been isolated, that the alarm had been inhibited, that the tank was not empty - and the person who acted did not. Four failure shapes cover most of it:

ul: Vertical - a junior officer or rating who sees the problem and does not challenge the senior. The information is present and suppressed.
Horizontal - between departments. The classic is engine and deck operating on different assumptions during manoeuvring, bunkering, cargo work or a blackout.
Handover - watch to watch, or joiner to leaver. What was temporary becomes permanent because the reason for it was never passed on.
Ship to shore - the office and the ship holding different pictures of the same situation, each believing the other has understood.
ISM Code 1.4.2 - the safety management system must define and document levels of authority and lines of communication between shore and shipboard personnel and among themselves.
ISM Code 6.6 - the Company shall establish procedures to ensure that ship's personnel receive relevant information on the safety management system in a working language understood by them.
ISM Code 6.7 - the Company shall ensure that ship's personnel are able to communicate effectively in the execution of their duties.

SOLAS regulation V/14 - a working language shall be established and recorded in the log book, and English is required on the bridge for safety communications where the working language is not a common one.

STCW Code section A-VIII/2 - watchkeeping arrangements, including bridge and engine-room resource management, which is where challenge, closed-loop communication and shared mental models are actually taught.
The Standard Marine Communication Phrases - a fixed vocabulary for exactly the situations in which improvised English fails.

blocks.p: Note that the requirement is capability, not declaration. The Code says personnel must be able to communicate effectively. A language written in a manual and not shared in practice does not satisfy it.

blocks.h: 8. Why present-day crewing makes this harder

ul: Multinational, multilingual crews are the norm. A declared working language is not the same as a shared one, and competence in a second language degrades fastest under stress - which is precisely when it is needed.
Short contracts and high turnover erode the informal knowledge that used to carry a ship - the things nobody wrote down because everybody had been there two years.

Power distance. Crews drawn from cultures with steep hierarchy, working under a Master or Chief from another, produce a real and measurable reluctance to challenge. Resource-management training exists for this reason.
Reduced manning and higher workload mean fewer people, each doing more, with less overlap in which to notice that a message did not land.
Fatigue degrades communication before it degrades anything else - the read-back is the first thing to go.

Shore intensity. Continuous connectivity gives the office a near-real-time picture and a stronger voice, which is useful, and which can also displace the judgement of the people who can actually see the ship.

And the two limbs meet here. A crew operating a fuel nobody aboard has run before is a crew whose cost of an ambiguous message has gone up. Poor communication and unfamiliar plant are not two separate problems; they multiply.

blocks.p: Two eight-mark limbs that look unrelated and are not. Limb (a) is about competence the industry assumes people have and has not taught them; limb (b) is about information the system assumes has arrived and has not. Closing limb (b) by joining the two - step 8's last bullet - is worth a mark on its own and almost nobody does it.

The highest-value discrimination in limb (a) is step 3: the mandatory training framework reaches the fuels we have had longest and not the ones that are new. A candidate who lists hazards without saying where the training obligation actually stops has written half the answer.

The hazard changed in kind, not in degree. You cannot make a battery safe by shutting a valve, you cannot see a methanol flame, and ammonia will have killed you before it catches fire. That is why existing competence does not scale into the new fuels, and it is why this is a training question rather than an equipment question.

ul: Writing limb (a) as a list of alternative fuels with no reference to competence or training at all.
Calling ammonia a zero-emission fuel. Unburnt slip and nitrous oxide are real and must be managed.
Treating the strategy as law. It sets a trajectory; the law running at this date is EEXI and the operational CII.
Claiming a carbon price or levy exists. None has been adopted.
Saying STCW already covers the new fuels. It covers ships subject to the IGF Code, and the newest fuels sit outside or at the edge of it.
Answering limb (b) as 'communication is important' with no instrument and no failure mode.
Confusing a declared working language with a shared one - the Code requires the ability to communicate effectively, not a language written in a manual.
'Is ammonia zero-emission?' No - unburnt ammonia slip and nitrous oxide production.
'What is the governing hazard with ammonia?' Toxicity, not fire. It is dangerous at concentrations far below the flammable range.
'What foam for a methanol fire?' Alcohol-resistant. Conventional foam breaks down.
'Does STCW require ammonia training?' Not through regulation V/3, which is tied to ships subject to the IGF Code.
'What does SOLAS require about language?' A working language established and recorded in the log book, with English for bridge safety communications where there is no common language.
'Your crew all declared English. Is that compliance?' Only if they can actually communicate effectively in the execution of their duties. Declaration is not capability.
What did the 2023 strategy replace and when was it adopted? The Initial Strategy of 2018, replaced at MEPC 80 in July 2023.

Which decarbonisation requirements are actually in force on your ship? EEXI and the operational CII under MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4, since 1 January 2023, with the SEEMP as the operational instrument.

How would you prepare a crew for a fuel none of them has run? Maker and simulator training, fuel-specific familiarisation beyond the Convention minimum, a fresh hazard identification with the ship's own staff, and drills written for the new hazard rather than adapted from the fire drill.

Where in the ISM Code is communication addressed? Element 1.4.2 for lines of authority and communication, 6.6 for a working language understood by the crew, and 6.7 for the ability to communicate effectively.

What is engine-room resource management and why does it matter? The structured use of all available people, information and equipment - and the licence for a junior to challenge a senior, which is what fails in the vertical failure mode.

blocks.p: Limb (a): hazard changed, driver, where training stops, fuel by fuel, and the non-fuel competences. Limb (b): causal not contributory, four failure shapes, the instruments, then crewing. Finish by joining them - unfamiliar plant raises the price of an ambiguous message.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Limb (a): THE HAZARD CHANGED IN KIND. Ammonia is toxic long before it is flammable and is NOT zero-emission (slip and nitrous oxide); methanol has an almost invisible flame and needs ALCOHOL-RESISTANT foam; hydrogen leaks through oil-tight joints and embrittles steel; batteries store energy you cannot valve off - thermal runaway and high voltage; LNG is cryogenic with boil-off. NO carbon price adopted. STCW V/3 and A-V/3 cover ships subject to the IGF CODE only - the newest fuels sit outside, so training is company-led. Limb (b): communication is CAUSAL - the information existed and did not arrive. Four shapes: vertical, horizontal, handover, ship-to-shore. Instruments: ISM 1.4.2, 6.6, 6.7; SOLAS V/14 working language in the log book, English on the bridge; STCW A-VIII/2 resource management; Standard Marine Communication Phrases. critical_numbers: 2023 GHG Strategy adopted 7 July 2023
EEXI and CII applicable from 1 January 2023

SOLAS regulation V/14
quick_revision.critical_regulation: ISM Code 6.7 - the Company shall ensure that ship's personnel are able to communicate effectively in the execution of their duties related to the safety management system. The obligation is CAPABILITY, not a declared language; 6.6 separately requires that safety management system information be given in a working language understood by the crew, and SOLAS regulation V/14 requires the working language to be established and recorded in the log book.
quick_revision.major_trap: Calling ammonia a zero-emission fuel, or asserting that STCW already mandates training for it. Ammonia produces unburnt slip and nitrous oxide, and regulation V/3 is tied to ships subject to the IGF Code, which is where the newest fuels sit outside the framework.

questions.memory_cue: Limb (a): kind not degree (1), driver (2), where training stops (3), fuels (4), non-fuel competences (5). Limb (b): causal (6), instruments (7), crewing (8) - then join them.
questions.understand_first: Both halves of this question are about something the system assumes people have and has not actually given them. On the fuels side the point is not that engineers must try harder at what they already know: it is that the danger has changed shape. Heavy fuel oil hurt you by burning, and everything the trade knows about fire-fighting, gas-freeing and hot work was built around that. The fuels now arriving hurt you differently. One poisons you at concentrations far below the level at which it would burn. One burns with a flame you cannot see in daylight. One escapes through joints that would comfortably hold oil, and makes the metal brittle on the way out. One holds its energy chemically, so there is no valve you can shut to make the space safe. Training built for the old hazard does not stretch to cover those. The other half is the same problem in a different form: on almost every ship that is lost, somebody aboard already knew the thing that would have prevented it, and that knowledge did not reach the person making the decision. That is why communication is described as a cause rather than as a courtesy - it is a link in the chain, and the modern crew, drawn from several countries on short contracts with fewer people aboard, has more places for the link to break.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the upskilling and communication question.
retrieval_cards.answer: Limb (a): 1 the hazard changed in kind. 2 the driver and what is actually in force. 3 where mandatory training stops. 4 fuel by fuel. 5 the non-fuel competences. Limb (b): 6 causal not contributory, with four failure shapes. 7 the instruments. 8 present-day crewing - closing by joining the two limbs.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (a) needs both an argument and specific examples; limb (b)'s crewing material is compulsory because the examiner named it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Is ammonia a zero-emission fuel, and what is its governing hazard?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Unburnt ammonia slip and nitrous oxide production mean it is not zero-emission in use. Its governing hazard is acute toxicity, not fire - it is dangerous at concentrations far below the flammable range, which inverts the whole fire-based safety model.
retrieval_cards.why: Both halves of this are commonly got wrong, and each is a clean mark.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which decarbonisation measures are policy and which are law at this date?
retrieval_cards.answer: The 2023 IMO GHG Strategy, adopted in July of this year, is policy - it sets the trajectory and the checkpoints. What is law and already running is MARPOL Annex VI chapter 4: EEXI and the operational carbon intensity indicator, applicable since 1 January, with this year the first data year so no ship has yet been rated. No market-based measure or carbon price has been adopted.
retrieval_cards.why: Presenting a strategy as an enforceable requirement is the commonest error on this subject.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does the mandatory training obligation for alternative fuels reach?
retrieval_cards.answer: STCW regulation V/3 and Code section A-V/3 set mandatory basic and advanced training for seafarers on ships subject to the IGF Code. Methanol ships operate under interim guidelines rather than a matured Code chapter, and ammonia and hydrogen have no adopted IMO safety guidelines at this date. The obligation is thinnest where the hazard is newest.
retrieval_cards.why: The sharpest available point on limb (a), and few candidates make it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the four shapes of communication failure found in casualty investigation.
retrieval_cards.answer: Vertical - the junior who sees it and does not challenge. Horizontal - between departments, classically engine and deck on different assumptions. Handover - watch to watch or joiner to leaver, where the temporary becomes permanent because the reason was not passed on. Ship to shore - office and ship holding different pictures of the same situation.
retrieval_cards.why: It converts 'communication is important' into a countable, analytical answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What do the instruments require about communication on board?
retrieval_cards.answer: ISM Code 1.4.2 - defined levels of authority and lines of communication. ISM 6.6 - safety management system information in a working language understood by the crew. ISM 6.7 - personnel able to communicate effectively in the execution of their duties. SOLAS regulation V/14 - a working language established and recorded in the log book, with English for bridge safety communications where there is no common language. STCW Code section A-VIII/2 - resource management. Plus the Standard Marine Communication Phrases.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (b) without instruments is an opinion; with them it is an answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Every crew member declared English. Does that satisfy the Code?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not by itself. The requirement in element 6.7 is that personnel are ABLE TO COMMUNICATE EFFECTIVELY in the execution of their duties. A declared working language that is not genuinely shared, and that degrades under stress, does not meet it.
retrieval_cards.why: Declaration against capability is the discrimination the limb is really testing.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do the two limbs of this question connect?
retrieval_cards.answer: A crew operating plant that nobody aboard has run before is a crew for whom the cost of an ambiguous message has risen. Unfamiliar fuel and weak communication are not two independent problems - they multiply, because there is no accumulated experience to catch the misunderstanding before it matters.
retrieval_cards.why: Closing on this earns a mark almost nobody collects.

questions.question_delta: IDENTICAL PRINTED STEM, EIGHT MONTHS EARLIER - the second-closest relation on this paper and by a wide margin the safest of the four exact relations available at any distance. The August 2024 answer was re-read in full and audited line by line. THE AUDIT FOUND ALMOST NOTHING TO REVERSE, and the reason is that the ISM Code itself has not been amended since MSC.353(92), whose amendments entered into force on 1 January 2015 - eight years before this sitting and unchanged at the donor's. The adoption chain, the functional requirements, the twelve Part A elements, the Part B certification layer and the continuous-improvement machinery in elements 9 and 12 are therefore identical at both sittings and transfer without qualification. The cyber-risk material also transfers intact: resolution MSC.428(98) was adopted in 2017 and required cyber risk to be addressed in the safety management system no later than the first annual verification of the Document of Compliance after 1 JANUARY 2021 - nearly three years before this sitting - so at December 2023 it is a MATURE requirement and not a novelty, and the answer says so. WHAT WAS CHECKED FOR AND REMOVED: any reference to the Merchant Shipping Act 2025 or DGMA; the MASS Code, adopted in May 2026 and the obvious later addition to an 'emerging challenges' limb; and any post-2023 decarbonisation instrument in the environmental-sustainability limb, where the answer's honest point is that the decarbonisation instruments sit OUTSIDE the Code in MARPOL Annex VI. blocks.h: 1. What the Code is, and how it binds

ul: The International Management Code for the Safe Operation of Ships and for Pollution Prevention, adopted by resolution A.741(18) and made mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX.
The operative text is the Code as amended through MSC.353(92), whose amendments entered into force on 1 January 2015. There has been no amendment to the Code since.
It regulates management, not construction or equipment. Every other safety instrument tells you something about the ship; this one tells you how the operation is to be run.

blocks.h: 2. What a safety management system is, and why the Code works through one

blocks.p: A safety management system is a structured and documented system enabling Company personnel to implement effectively the Company's safety and environmental protection policy. The Code sets objectives and requires a system; it does not write the procedures - because the right procedure for a product tanker is not the right procedure for a bulk carrier.

That is the answer to limb (a)'s opening question. The system is not a by-product of the Code; it is the instrument through which the Code operates. Without it the Code is a statement of intent with nothing to inspect.
Element 1.4 requires every safety management system to include:

ul: a safety and environmental protection policy;
instructions and procedures to ensure safe operation of ships and protection of the environment, in compliance with relevant international and flag State legislation;
defined levels of authority and lines of communication between and among shore and shipboard personnel;
procedures for reporting accidents and non-conformities with the provisions of the Code;
procedures to prepare for and respond to emergency situations;
procedures for internal audits and management reviews.

blocks.p: Six is a countable list and the examiner will count it. Note that the last two are the continuous-improvement machinery appearing already at the functional level.
