blocks.p: Part B is the certification layer - elements 13 to 16: certification and periodical verification, interim certification, verification, and the forms of certificates.

ul: Document of Compliance to the Company, valid up to five years, verified annually within three months of the anniversary date.
Safety Management Certificate to the ship, valid up to five years, with an intermediate verification between the second and third anniversary.
Interim certification for a new company, a new ship type or a newly delivered ship.
A major non-conformity requires immediate corrective action and can lead to withdrawal of the certificate - which is what gives the Code its teeth.

blocks.h: 5. The role the system plays in implementing the Code

ul: It converts objectives into procedures that a named person performs. Element 3 requires the Company to define and document responsibility, authority and interrelation of all personnel.
It creates the shore-to-ship link through the Designated Person, who has direct access to the highest level of management - the single structural innovation of the Code.

It preserves the Master's overriding authority to make decisions for safety and pollution prevention and to request the Company's assistance, so that the system can never be used to override his judgement.
It generates the evidence on which compliance is verified. Audit is possible only because the system produces records.

blocks.h: 6. Continuous improvement - the mechanism, and why it is the significant part

blocks.p: The examiner has asked specifically for the significance of continuous improvement, so name the machinery and then say why it matters.

ul: Element 9 - procedures for reporting non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences, their investigation and analysis, and corrective action to prevent recurrence. Near-miss reporting lives here, and it is the input that keeps the system honest.

Element 12 - the Company carries out internal safety audits at intervals not exceeding twelve months, periodically evaluates the effectiveness of the system, and requires timely corrective action by personnel responsible.
Element 5 - the Master's own periodic review of the system and his reporting of deficiencies to shore management.
Management review at Company level closes the loop, because a defect the ship cannot fix has to reach somebody who can.

blocks.p: Why it is the significant part: without it a safety management system becomes a static manual describing a ship nobody operates. Continuous improvement is what makes the system self-correcting rather than merely documented - and it is the difference between a certified company and a safe one. It is also the reason the Code has needed so few amendments: a system required to examine and correct itself absorbs change that a prescriptive rule would have to be rewritten to accommodate.

blocks.h: 7. Why the Code exists, and the shift it represents

blocks.p: Limb (b) begins properly with the reason, because every later evolution follows from it. The Code came out of a major ro-ro passenger casualty and an inquiry that found the fault ashore as much as aboard - in how the operation was managed rather than in how the ship was built.

ul: From regulating hardware to regulating management.
From compliance demonstrated by inspection of the ship to compliance demonstrated by an auditable system.
From the ship alone to the Company ashore, which is why the Document of Compliance is issued to the Company and not to the vessel.

From recommendation to mandatory instrument. Adopted as an Assembly resolution, then made mandatory through SOLAS chapter IX and phased in by ship type. This is the single largest change in its history.

The amendment chain. MSC.104(73), MSC.179(79), MSC.195(80), MSC.273(85) and MSC.353(92) - successively tightening company responsibility, the handling of non-conformities, risk assessment wording and internal audit. The current text has been in force since 1 January 2015 and is the operative one at this examination.

Technological advancement. Integrated bridge and engine control, remote monitoring and diagnostics, condition-based maintenance and electronic record-keeping. The Code accommodated all of it without amendment, through elements 6, 7 and 10 - resources and personnel, shipboard operations, and maintenance. Familiarisation and competence, not the technology, become the binding constraint.

Cyber risk. Resolution MSC.428(98), adopted 16 June 2017, affirms that an approved safety management system should take cyber risk into account, and requires it to be appropriately addressed no later than the first annual verification of the Document of Compliance after 1 January 2021 - so at this examination it is a mature requirement, verified for nearly three years, not a novelty. No new element was added to the Code. The existing risk-assessment and procedures machinery was used, which is a demonstration of the Code's method rather than an exception to it.

Environmental sustainability - and the honest limit. Environmental protection is in the Code's title and in its objectives from the beginning, and element 7 procedures cover pollution-prevention operations. But the instruments that actually drive environmental performance sit outside the Code, in MARPOL Annex VI - the ship energy efficiency management plan and the carbon-intensity requirements that have applied since 1 January this year. The Code adapts by generality, which is both its strength and its weakness: it can absorb a new risk without amendment, and it therefore says nothing specific about any of them.

blocks.p: The closing judgement, which is what 'examine' is asking for: the Code has evolved far less in its text than in what it is asked to cover, and it has survived because it regulates a process rather than a hazard. A process requirement absorbs new hazards; a hazard-specific rule has to be rewritten for each one.

Eight and eight. Limb (a) has three named tasks - role, components, and the significance of continuous improvement - and the components are the part candidates over-write, because listing twelve elements feels productive. It is worth roughly a third of the limb; steps 5 and 6 carry the rest and are where the examiner's word role and significance are actually answered.

Limb (b) names three challenges - technology, cyber, environment - and the strongest answer treats them as a test of the Code's method rather than as three paragraphs. The Code met all three without amending its text; saying why is the judgement mark.

Every safety rule written before this one told you something about the ship: how thick the steel, how many boats, what the fire pumps must deliver. Inspect the ship and you knew whether the rule had been obeyed. But ships kept being lost that satisfied every one of those requirements, and the failure lay in how the operation was run - and often ashore. This Code regulates that instead. Because it regulates a process rather than a hazard, it absorbs new hazards without being rewritten.

ul: Listing the twelve elements and calling that the answer to 'the role of the system'.
Giving five or seven functional requirements. There are six.
Putting the Document of Compliance on the ship. It goes to the Company; the ship holds the Safety Management Certificate.
Saying the Code was amended to deal with cyber risk. It was not - a separate resolution required cyber risk to be handled inside the existing system.
Claiming the Code contains the decarbonisation requirements. It does not - those are in MARPOL Annex VI.
Treating continuous improvement as a slogan rather than naming elements 9 and 12 and the twelve-month audit interval.
Forgetting the Master's overriding authority, which is the safeguard that makes the rest of the system acceptable.
'How many functional requirements?' Six.
'Who holds the Document of Compliance?' The Company. Up to five years, verified annually.
'How often is an internal audit?' At intervals not exceeding twelve months.
'Was the Code amended for cyber risk?' No. A separate resolution required it to be addressed within the existing system, by the first annual Document of Compliance verification after 1 January 2021.

'What is a major non-conformity?' A deviation posing a serious threat to personnel or the ship, or a serious risk to the environment, requiring immediate corrective action - and capable of costing the certificate.
'Can the Company overrule the Master on a safety decision?' No. His overriding authority is in element 5.

What does element 10.3 require? Identification of equipment and technical systems whose sudden operational failure may result in hazardous situations, with specific measures to promote their reliability.

Who is the Designated Person and what makes the role unusual? A person ashore with direct access to the highest level of management, providing a link between the Company and those on board that bypasses the normal chain.

How does a near miss improve the system? Element 9 requires it to be reported, investigated and analysed, with corrective action to prevent recurrence - it is free information about a failure that has not yet cost anything.
Which certificate is verified at an intermediate verification, and when? The Safety Management Certificate, between the second and third anniversary date.
Why has the Code needed so few amendments? Because it regulates a process that is required to examine and correct itself, so new hazards are absorbed rather than legislated for.

blocks.p: Limb (a): what it is, what a system is, six requirements, components, role, improvement. Limb (b): why it exists, then five evolutions - mandatory, amendments, technology, cyber, environment. Close on the judgement: it regulates a process, not a hazard.

questions.understand_first: Every rule of maritime safety written before this one told you something about the ship: how thick the steel, how many boats, how the bulkheads were arranged, what the fire pumps must deliver. You could inspect the ship and know whether the rule had been obeyed. But ships kept being lost that satisfied every one of those requirements, and when the losses were investigated the failure was repeatedly found not in the hardware, and often not even entirely on board. It lay in how the operation was run - nobody had written down who was responsible for what, the people ashore were pressing commercially and nobody could say no, and the lesson from the last near miss had never reached anyone who could act on it. So this Code regulates the running of the ship instead of the building of her. It does not write the procedures, because the right procedure differs from trade to trade; it requires the company to have a documented system, to say who does what, and then to keep checking and correcting that system itself. That last part is what makes it work, and it is also why the Code has hardly changed its wording in thirty years while the things it has to cover - new technology, computers that can be attacked, environmental performance - have changed completely. A rule about a process can absorb a new hazard. A rule about a hazard has to be rewritten for each one.

blocks.h: 1. The three cost families, and what distinguishes them

blocks.p: The families are separated by what makes the money go out - not by how large they are. That single test is what lets the Chief Engineer see where he has leverage:

rows: Capital
Owning the ship at all
Fixed, and committed before she ever traded
Operating
Keeping her manned, maintained and fit to trade
Largely fixed per day, incurred whether or not she is employed
Voyage
Performing a particular voyage
Variable - it stops when the voyage stops

ul: Capital - the newbuilding or purchase price, debt service and interest, depreciation, and the return the owner requires on his equity. A major capital improvement belongs here, not in maintenance.

Operating - crew wages, victualling and travel; stores and consumables including lubricating oil and chemicals; spares; repairs and maintenance; drydocking and survey costs; hull and machinery insurance and protection and indemnity cover; registration and flag fees; and shore management and administration.

Voyage - bunker fuel, which normally dominates; port dues and charges; canal transit dues; and pilotage and towage. Cargo-handling costs are treated by some texts as a fourth family; they are taken here as voyage-related, and the convention is stated rather than assumed.

blocks.p: Bunkers are a voyage cost, not an operating cost. They are triggered by performing the voyage and they cease when she stops. Misclassifying them is the commonest single error on this question.

blocks.h: 3. Where the Chief Engineer has leverage - and where he has none

blocks.p: Being candid about this is what separates a management answer from a list.

ul: Capital - effectively no short-run influence. The price was paid and the loan signed before he joined. His effect is indirect and long-term: through the condition in which the ship is kept, her residual value, and the technical advice he gives on a major upgrade.
Voyage - his largest lever, because fuel dominates the voyage account, and fuel consumption is a direct function of hull and machinery condition and of how the plant is operated.
Operating - shared with the office. Crew cost, insurance and flag fees are set ashore. Maintenance, spares, stores, lubricating oil and the drydock specification are substantially his.

Hull and propeller condition. Fouling raises the power needed for a given speed and is usually the largest single recoverable loss on a ship. Systematic performance monitoring normalised for draught, weather and speed; timely propeller polishing and hull cleaning; and a coating specification matched to the actual trade.

Machinery condition and performance. Indicator and pressure-rise data, turbocharger condition, air and gas differential pressures, cooler and economiser fouling - each degradation shows up as fuel before it shows up as a defect.

Correct operation for the loading in use. Slow steaming saves fuel but moves the engine into a region it was not optimised for; running there without the appropriate measures costs more in wear than it saves in fuel.
Fuel management. Bunker quantity survey and sampling at delivery, correct treatment and settling, avoidance of commingling incompatible fuels, and minimising unpumpable residues.
Auxiliary and hotel load. Generator loading, boiler and steam management, shaft generator use where fitted, and load reduction in port.

The regulatory overlay - and what it is not. Under MARPOL Annex VI regulations 23, 25 and 28, EEXI and the operational carbon intensity indicator have applied since 1 January this year, so efficiency is now a compliance outcome and a data-integrity obligation and not merely a cost. 2023 is the first data year, so no ship has yet been assigned a rating. There is no carbon price of any kind reaching this voyage account - no IMO market-based measure has been adopted, and the European emissions trading scheme does not extend to shipping until the first of next month.

Maintenance strategy. Breakdown maintenance is the most expensive way to run machinery; time-based maintenance overhauls items that were still serviceable; condition-based maintenance spends the money when the evidence says it is needed. The real contribution is choosing the right strategy for each item rather than applying one to all.

Off-hire avoidance. A day off-hire usually costs more than the repair that caused it, because the daily operating cost continues while the revenue stops. Ranking maintenance by the consequence of failure rather than by the price of the part follows directly from that.
Lubricating oil management. Feed-rate optimisation, the correct base number for the fuel in use, and onboard and laboratory analysis to catch wear early.

Drydock specification. The docking is the single largest operating-cost event the Chief Engineer materially controls, and a specification written from real condition data rather than repeated from last time is where the money is saved or lost.
Spares and stores control - which is the third task in the question.

blocks.p: Modern inventory control begins by recognising that not every item deserves the same control. The techniques are ways of deciding which item gets which treatment.

rows: ABC analysis
Annual consumption value
Concentrating control effort on the few items carrying most of the money
VED analysis
Criticality - Vital, Essential, Desirable
Deciding what must never be out of stock, regardless of price
FSN analysis
Movement - Fast, Slow, Non-moving
Finding dead stock and obsolescence
SDE analysis
Procurement difficulty - Scarce, Difficult, Easy
Setting safety stock by how hard the item is to obtain

blocks.p: The important move is to combine them. ABC alone will under-protect a cheap but vital item; VED alone will over-protect an expensive but non-critical one. The practical shipboard method is the ABC-VED matrix, and the criticality axis is anchored in ISM Code element 10.3, which requires the Company to identify equipment and technical systems whose sudden operational failure may result in hazardous situations, and to provide specific measures promoting their reliability. That identification is the ship's own authoritative definition of a 'Vital' item.

blocks.h: 7. Inventory control - ordering, and the limits of just-in-time at sea

ul: Economic order quantity balances the cost of ordering against the cost of holding and gives the order size at which their sum is least. A useful idea, but it assumes steady demand and a stable lead time.

Reorder level and minimum-maximum. Reorder level is average consumption over the lead time plus a safety stock. On a ship the lead time is the hard variable, because it depends on where the ship will be, not on how quickly the supplier can act.
Safety stock buffers variability in both demand and lead time, and should be set by criticality rather than uniformly.

Lead-time and voyage-plan integration. Ordering is planned against the trading pattern so deliveries fall where the ship will actually be, and against the maintenance plan so parts arrive before the overhaul rather than after it.
Standardisation and fleet pooling. Common makers and models across a fleet cut the number of distinct items held and let stock be shared between ships.
Vendor-managed inventory and framework agreements with makers and service providers, which move some holding cost and obsolescence risk onto the supplier.
Digital stock control integrated with the planned maintenance system, so that consumption, criticality and the maintenance schedule are read from one record rather than three.

blocks.p: Just-in-time deserves a qualification, not a recommendation. Minimising holding is sound for consumables and for non-critical items obtainable worldwide. It is wrong for critical spares: a ship is not a factory beside a motorway, the lead time is measured in ports rather than hours, and the consequence of a stock-out is an unseaworthy ship rather than an idle production line. The correct answer is selective - just-in-time where the item is easy and the failure tolerable, and protected stock where element 10.3 says the failure is not.

Three tasks in one unlimbed question, roughly a third of the marks each. The failure mode is predictable: candidates write at length on the cost families, moderately on the Chief Engineer's role, and then produce two lines on inventory control because the time has gone. Steps 6 and 7 are a full third of the question and the route is built so they are reached with time in hand.

Step 3 - being candid about where the Chief Engineer has no influence - is what makes this read as a management answer rather than a recitation. Saying plainly that capital cost is beyond his short-run reach earns more credit than inventing influence he does not have.

Classify by trigger, not by size. Capital is triggered by owning, operating by keeping her fit to trade, voyage by performing the voyage. Once costs are classified that way you can see immediately which ones stop when the ship stops - and therefore which ones the person running the machinery can actually move. Inventory control is the same idea applied to stock: decide what each item deserves before deciding how much of it to hold.

ul: Classing bunkers as an operating cost. They are a voyage cost.
Listing the three families and never answering the second and third tasks.
Claiming the Chief Engineer optimises capital cost. He does not, in any short-run sense.
Naming ABC and VED without saying what each classifies by, or how they are used together.
Recommending just-in-time for critical spares without qualification.
Treating drydock cost as unavoidable. The specification is where it is decided.
Forgetting that cargo-handling costs are treated differently by different texts - say which convention you are using.
'Is fuel a voyage or an operating cost?' Voyage. The commonest single trap on the question.
'Would you apply just-in-time on board?' Selectively - and never to items identified under element 10.3.
'ABC says this item is class C. Do you let it run out?' Not if VED says it is Vital. That is exactly why the two are combined.
'What is the largest recoverable fuel loss on a ship?' Usually hull and propeller fouling.
'What happens to costs when the ship goes off-hire?' The daily operating cost continues while the revenue stops - which is why off-hire avoidance dominates the arithmetic.

'Does a carbon cost appear in your voyage account?' Not at this date. No market-based measure has been adopted internationally, and the European scheme does not reach shipping until the first of next month.
Which costs continue when the ship is laid up? Capital and most operating costs; voyage costs cease.
How would you set the safety stock for a turbocharger spare? By criticality under VED and procurement difficulty under SDE - not by its price.
What does element 10.3 require? Identification of equipment whose sudden operational failure may result in hazardous situations, with specific measures to promote reliability.
Name three maintenance strategies and say when each is right. Breakdown, time-based and condition-based - chosen per item by the consequence of failure.
How do you demonstrate that a fuel saving is real? Systematic performance monitoring normalised for draught, weather and speed.

blocks.p: C-O-V for the families, then trigger, contents, leverage for each. For inventory, two moves: classify, then order. Classify with ABC-VED-FSN-SDE; order with EOQ, reorder level, safety stock, lead time. Finish with the just-in-time qualification, which is the mark that shows judgement.

Operating cost is shared with the office - crew, insurance and flag fees are set ashore, while maintenance, spares, stores, lubricating oil and the drydock specification are substantially his.
retrieval_cards.why: The candour about capital is what makes this a management answer rather than a list.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the inventory classification techniques and say what each classifies by.
retrieval_cards.answer: ABC by annual consumption value; VED by criticality - Vital, Essential, Desirable; FSN by movement - Fast, Slow, Non-moving; SDE by procurement difficulty - Scarce, Difficult, Easy. The practical shipboard method combines ABC with VED in a matrix.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming without the classifying basis earns little; the combination is the marks-bearing insight.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the ISM Code enter an inventory-control answer?
retrieval_cards.answer: Element 10.3 requires the Company to identify equipment and technical systems whose sudden operational failure may result in hazardous situations, and to provide specific measures promoting their reliability. That identification is the ship's own authoritative definition of a 'Vital' item for VED classification and of what must never be allowed to run out.
retrieval_cards.why: It converts a management technique into a regulated obligation, which is exactly the level a Class I answer should reach.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Should just-in-time be applied to shipboard spares?
retrieval_cards.answer: Selectively. It is sound for consumables and non-critical items obtainable worldwide. It is wrong for critical spares: lead time is measured in ports rather than hours, and a stock-out produces an unseaworthy ship rather than an idle line. Items identified under element 10.3 must carry protected stock.
retrieval_cards.why: The qualification is the judgement mark; an unqualified recommendation is the classic error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does a carbon cost appear in the voyage account at this date?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. No international market-based measure has been adopted, and the regional European emissions trading scheme does not extend to shipping until the first of next month. Efficiency is nonetheless already a compliance obligation, through EEXI and the operational carbon intensity indicator, which have applied since 1 January this year.
retrieval_cards.why: Distinguishing a compliance obligation from a price is the discrimination, and both halves are specific to this sitting.

blocks.h: 1. The accurate starting point - critical habitat, but not a designated area

blocks.p: The wording of the question invites an error, and the first mark is for not making it. Both island groups are unquestionably critical habitat - coral atolls and reefs, seagrass beds, mangrove, turtle nesting beaches and endemic species - and both carry substantial protection under Indian domestic law.

But neither group is a designated IMO Particularly Sensitive Sea Area. Designations worldwide are few, the first being the Great Barrier Reef in 1990, and none of them is in Indian waters. No Indian sea area is a MARPOL Special Area and none is an Emission Control Area either.

That is precisely why the stem asks how these islands could be protected. The answer is properly a programme of measures - some already in place domestically, some India would have to seek internationally - and the discrimination this limb rewards is between an environmentally sensitive area and a formally designated area under an international instrument.

blocks.h: 2. The Indian statutory and administrative layer

ul: Ship-source pollution - the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958, which carries the prevention and containment of pollution of the sea by oil, with the Merchant Shipping Rules as the working detail, administered by DG Shipping.

Coastal and island zoning - the Island Coastal Regulation Zone Notification, 2019, made under section 3 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, which applies specifically to the Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep groups and superseded the earlier island protection zone notification. It classifies coastal stretches into zones of decreasing sensitivity and restricts what may be done in each.
Habitat protection - marine national parks and wildlife sanctuaries under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972, which operates independently of the shipping regime.

Jurisdictional reach - the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and Other Maritime Zones Act, 1976, which is what makes a measure in the exclusive economic zone legally available at all.

Response - the Indian Coast Guard under the Coast Guard Act, 1978 as central coordinating authority for oil spill response, with the national oil spill disaster contingency plan - and the practical difficulty that these are remote archipelagos a long way from the mainland response bases.
Port reception facilities and port State control of ships calling, which is what closes the loop between a discharge requirement on paper and what a ship actually does.

blocks.h: 3. The international measures India could seek

blocks.p: Each has a named legal basis, and naming it is the difference between a list of wishes and an answer.

blocks.p: Above all of these sits UNCLOS article 194(5), the obligation on States to take measures necessary to protect and preserve rare or fragile ecosystems and the habitat of depleted, threatened or endangered species. That is the general duty from which the specific measures draw their justification.

blocks.h: 4. What a coherent programme would look like, in sequence

ul: Establish the science and the traffic picture. Habitat and reef-condition surveys, and a study of the vessel types, tonnages, cargoes and traffic density actually passing. Without the traffic evidence no international proposal can succeed, for the reason in step 7.
Apply the domestic controls already available - the island coastal zone notification, the wildlife legislation, and the pollution provisions of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 and its rules.

Build the response and reception capability first - reception facilities at island ports, pre-positioned response equipment and exercised plans - because Special Area status depends on it and a discharge prohibition without a place to discharge legally is unenforceable.
Seek the international measures - a PSSA supported by an area to be avoided and mandatory reporting, or Special Area status, with compulsory pilotage in the confined approaches.
Chart, promulgate and enforce. A measure that is not on the chart does not change what a master does.

blocks.h: 5. What a Particularly Sensitive Sea Area is - and what it is not

ul: An area that needs special protection through action by IMO because of its recognised ecological, socio-economic or scientific significance, and because it may be vulnerable to damage by international shipping activities.
The governing instrument is resolution A.982(24), the Revised PSSA Guidelines, as amended by MEPC.267(68).
It is a designation by IMO, not a declaration by the coastal State - which is what distinguishes it from a national marine protected area, and is the reason India could not simply declare one.
Decisively: a PSSA has no legal effect of its own. What regulates shipping is the Associated Protective Measure. A PSSA without an APM changes nothing that a ship must do.

blocks.p: That last point is the single highest-value proposition in limb (b), and most candidates miss it entirely.

blocks.h: 6. The criteria for identification - three groups, and one is enough

blocks.p: The Guidelines set the criteria in three groups, and an area must meet at least one - not all three.

ul: Ecological - uniqueness or rarity; critical habitat; dependency; representativeness; diversity; productivity; spawning or breeding grounds; naturalness; integrity; fragility; and bio-geographic importance.
Social, cultural and economic - social or economic dependency; human dependency, including of indigenous and local populations; and cultural heritage.
Scientific and educational - research value; use for baseline and monitoring studies; and educational value.

blocks.p: The Indian islands would satisfy several without difficulty. Meeting a criterion is not the hard part - which is why the next step matters more.

blocks.h: 7. The vulnerability test - where proposals actually fail

blocks.p: Meeting a criterion is necessary but not sufficient. The proposal must also demonstrate vulnerability to damage by international shipping activities, and this is a separate test.

ul: Vessel traffic characteristics - operational factors, the types of vessel, traffic density and routeing, and the harmful substances carried.

Natural factors - hydrographical conditions such as depth, seabed and confined channels; meteorological conditions such as wind, current, visibility and cyclone exposure; and oceanographic conditions determining where a spill would actually go.

blocks.p: A precious reef with no shipping near it fails the test, because IMO's jurisdiction is over ships and not over ecosystems. For the Indian islands the argument is strong: proximity to major east-west trade routes, laden tanker traffic passing close by, remoteness from response resources, cyclone exposure and confined reef approaches.

blocks.h: 8. The designation procedure, and the associated protective measure

ul: Only a Member Government may propose. The application goes to the Marine Environment Protection Committee and must describe the area, show that at least one criterion is met, demonstrate vulnerability to international shipping, and propose at least one Associated Protective Measure.

Every APM must have an identified legal basis - a routeing measure under SOLAS V/10, a reporting system under V/11, a discharge restriction or Special Area under MARPOL, compulsory pilotage, a measure adopted by IMO in its own right, or a measure under UNCLOS article 211(6).
The Committee may grant designation in principle once satisfied on the criteria and on vulnerability.

The APM is then referred to the appropriate IMO body - routeing and reporting measures to the navigation sub-committee and the Maritime Safety Committee; discharge measures to the environment committee itself.
Once the APM is adopted, final designation is granted.
The area and its measures are then charted and promulgated, so that mariners can see them and comply.

blocks.p: Eight and eight. Limb (a) looks like a description and is actually a trap wearing the clothes of a description: it names two famously precious island groups and invites you to describe how well protected they are. The first mark is for knowing that neither is a designated Particularly Sensitive Sea Area, that no Indian sea area is, and that none is a MARPOL Special Area either. Everything after that follows from answering the question actually asked - how they could be protected.

Limb (b) has three tasks hidden in two sentences: what a PSSA is, the criteria for identification, and the criteria for designation. Identification and designation are not the same step, and separating them - criteria, then vulnerability, then procedure - is what earns the second half of the limb.

Two layers of law protect a sea area and they come from opposite directions. Domestic law protects the place: India can zone its own coasts, declare its own sanctuaries and police its own waters, and it has done all three. International law protects it from ships, and only IMO can do that, because a ship of another flag is not bound by an Indian notification when she is passing. That is why the answer to 'how could these islands be protected' is a programme with two halves, and why the international half has to be applied for rather than declared.

ul: Describing the islands as a PSSA. They are not, and none of the designated areas is in Indian waters.
Calling them a MARPOL Special Area. No Indian sea area is.
Answering limb (a) as a description of an existing regime rather than as a programme of what could be done.
Mixing the domestic and international layers so that it is unclear which measure comes from where.
Saying a PSSA prohibits discharges or restricts navigation of itself. It does not - the Associated Protective Measure does all the regulating.
Listing criteria without the vulnerability test, which is a separate requirement and is where proposals actually fail.
Saying an area must meet all the criteria. It must meet at least one.
Forgetting that only a Member Government may propose, and that the proposal must include at least one APM with an identified legal basis.
'Are the Andamans a PSSA?' No. None of the designated areas is in Indian waters.
'What does a PSSA actually prohibit?' Nothing by itself. The Associated Protective Measure does the regulating; a PSSA without an APM changes nothing a ship must do.
'How many criteria must be met?' At least one of the three groups - not all.
'The reef is precious and there is no traffic near it. Can it be a PSSA?' No - it would fail the vulnerability test, because IMO's jurisdiction is over ships.
'Who can propose one?' Only a Member Government, to the environment committee.
'What stops a Special Area working?' The absence of adequate reception facilities.

Name three associated protective measures and their legal bases. An area to be avoided under SOLAS V/10; a mandatory reporting system under SOLAS V/11; a discharge restriction or Special Area under MARPOL. Compulsory pilotage and UNCLOS article 211(6) measures are the others.
Which was the first PSSA and when? The Great Barrier Reef, in 1990.

What does the Island Coastal Regulation Zone Notification do? Made under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, it zones the coastal stretches of these two island groups by sensitivity and restricts activity in each zone.
Who coordinates an oil spill response in Indian waters? The Indian Coast Guard, under the national oil spill contingency plan.
Why does a no-anchoring area matter around coral? Anchor and chain damage to coral is direct physical destruction and is one of the harms routeing measures can actually stop.

blocks.p: Limb (a): not designated, domestic layer, international options, programme in sequence. Limb (b): what it is, criteria, vulnerability, procedure. The single sentence to carry into the room is that a PSSA regulates nothing by itself - the associated measure does.

questions.understand_first: This question looks like an invitation to describe how well protected two famously precious island groups are. It is not. The opening move that earns the first mark is a correction: these islands are genuinely critical habitat and they are extensively protected under national law, but neither has any designation under an international instrument at all, and nor does any Indian sea area. That is exactly why the question asks how they could be protected rather than how they are. So the answer is a plan, and it has two halves that come from opposite directions. A country can zone its own coasts, declare its own sanctuaries and police its own waters - but a ship flying somebody else's flag passing offshore is not bound by any of that, and only the international body can reach her. So the domestic half is available immediately and the international half has to be applied for. And the second limb turns on a distinction that sounds like a technicality and is not: giving an area a protective label does not by itself change a single thing a ship must do. The label identifies the area; a separate, specific measure - keep out of this box, report before you enter, do not discharge here, take a pilot - is what actually regulates. An area with the label and no measure is a designation with nothing behind it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does a PSSA designation actually prohibit?
retrieval_cards.answer: Nothing of itself. A PSSA has no legal effect on its own; what regulates shipping is the Associated Protective Measure - a routeing measure, a reporting system, a discharge restriction, compulsory pilotage or a measure under UNCLOS article 211(6). A PSSA without an APM changes nothing that a ship must do.
retrieval_cards.why: The single highest-value proposition in limb (b), and most candidates miss it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the three groups of PSSA criteria, and say how many must be met.
retrieval_cards.answer: Ecological - uniqueness or rarity, critical habitat, dependency, representativeness, diversity, productivity, spawning or breeding grounds, naturalness, integrity, fragility and bio-geographic importance. Social, cultural and economic - social or economic dependency, human dependency including of indigenous and local populations, and cultural heritage. Scientific and educational - research value, baseline and monitoring value, and educational value. At least ONE must be met, not all three.
retrieval_cards.why: Saying all criteria must be met is a clean and common error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is the vulnerability test separate from the criteria, and what does it examine?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because meeting a criterion is necessary but not sufficient - the proposal must also demonstrate vulnerability to damage by international shipping activities. It examines vessel traffic characteristics - types of vessel, density, routeing and the harmful substances carried - and natural factors: hydrographical, meteorological and oceanographic conditions. A precious reef with no shipping near it fails, because IMO's jurisdiction is over ships.
retrieval_cards.why: This is where real proposals fail, and separating it from the criteria is what earns the second half of limb (b).

retrieval_cards.prompt: Outline the PSSA designation procedure.
retrieval_cards.answer: Only a Member Government may propose. The application goes to the environment committee and must describe the area, show at least one criterion is met, demonstrate vulnerability to international shipping, and propose at least one Associated Protective Measure with an identified legal basis. The committee may grant designation in principle; the APM is referred to the appropriate IMO body - routeing and reporting to the navigation sub-committee and the Maritime Safety Committee, discharge measures to the environment committee itself - and once it is adopted, final designation is granted. The area and its measures are then charted and promulgated.
retrieval_cards.why: The two-stage structure - in principle, then final once the measure exists - is the procedural mark.

blocks.h: 1. What a classification society is, and its two distinct roles

ul: A body that publishes rules for the design, construction and maintenance of ships, and assigns and maintains class to ships built and kept to those rules. Its origin is the underwriters' need for an independent technical judgement of a ship they were being asked to insure.
Role one - classification. Private and contractual, between the society and the owner. It is not a public law function.

Role two - statutory work. Where the flag State delegates statutory survey and certification to it, the society acts as a recognized organization, recognized under SOLAS regulation XI-1/1 and governed by the RO Code, which has been mandatory since 1 January 2015.

The Administration retains responsibility. Delegation transfers the work, not the duty - which is why the RO Code imposes oversight obligations on the flag State as well as requirements on the society.

blocks.p: Keeping these two roles apart is the first discrimination on the question, because the SOLAS point in the second half of limb (a) is precisely about the first role being given legal effect.

ul: Service experience - defect and damage returns from the surveyed fleet, which is the society's largest single advantage: it sees what actually fails, in what service, at what age.
Casualty investigation feedback, both its own and the flag States'.
Research and direct calculation - finite element analysis, fatigue assessment, direct strength analysis and full-scale measurement.
Technical committees of owners, builders, makers and the society's own surveyors, which is how practical experience reaches the drafting.

Harmonisation through the association of classification societies - unified requirements which member societies must incorporate, unified interpretations of statutory instruments, and procedural requirements governing how the societies work.
The Common Structural Rules for Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers - a single harmonised set for the two ship types where competitive rule differences had most cost the industry.

Scantlings, section modulus and hull girder strength; loading conditions and permissible still-water and wave bending; fatigue life; corrosion additions and coating requirements; close-up survey and thickness measurement regimes

Construction - material certification, welder and welding-procedure qualification, non-destructive testing and tank testing witnessed, survey during construction, and attendance at trials.

In service - the class survey cycle: annual, intermediate and renewal surveys of hull and machinery, bottom and docking surveys, tailshaft surveys and boiler surveys, with continuous survey of machinery and an approved planned maintenance scheme available as alternatives.
Enforcement - condition of class imposing a defined action by a defined date; and suspension or withdrawal of class where it is not met or where a serious defect is not repaired.

blocks.h: 5. Why compliance is now mentioned in SOLAS chapter II-1

blocks.p: The provision is regulation II-1/3-1, and the reason it exists repays being stated carefully.

ul: SOLAS never contained scantling rules. It has a great deal to say about subdivision, stability, fire protection and life-saving, and nothing at all about how thick a plate must be. Hull strength was the classification societies' private business with the owner and the underwriter.

So class was commercially indispensable but legally optional: a ship could satisfy every word of SOLAS and still be structurally substandard, and losing class was an insurance and chartering problem rather than a breach of the Convention.

Regulation II-1/3-1 closed that gap by pointing SOLAS at the private rule book. Ships shall be designed, constructed and maintained in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a classification society recognized by the Administration under regulation XI-1/1, or with applicable national standards of the Administration providing an equivalent level of safety.

The word that does the work is 'maintained'. The obligation is not discharged at delivery; it runs for the ship's whole life. Loss of class therefore became a SOLAS non-compliance, enforceable by the flag State and inspectable by port State control.

The alternative route matters too. An Administration may use its own national standards, but they must provide an equivalent level of safety - so the regulation compels a recognised technical standard without compelling membership of any particular society.

And it connects forward. For bulk carriers and oil tankers of 150 m and above, regulation II-1/3-10 goes further and requires that the society's rules themselves have been verified as conforming to goals set by IMO. II-1/3-1 points at the rule book; II-1/3-10 audits it.

blocks.h: 6. The harmonized system, and where these surveys sit

blocks.p: Limb (b) is worth the same eight marks as limb (a) on this paper, so the survey material is developed rather than sketched.

ul: The harmonized system was introduced by the 1988 SOLAS and Load Lines Protocols and extended to the MARPOL Annexes by later environment committee amendments.

What it harmonised: a common five-year certificate cycle, common anniversary dates across the certificates, a survey window of three months either side of the due date, and the ability to combine surveys into a single attendance instead of a succession of separate visits.
The survey types are initial, annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal and additional, together with the inspection of the ship's bottom.

The recommended practice for carrying them out is set out in the IMO Survey Guidelines under the Harmonized System, revised periodically by the Assembly. The edition in circulation at this sitting is the one adopted by the 32nd Assembly in 2021; the 33rd Assembly adopted a 2023 revision on 6 December 2023, within the month of this examination, and no claim is made here about which side of that date the paper was sat. Nothing in this answer depends on it, because the Guidelines are recommendatory - the resolution invites Governments to apply them - and the obligation to survey comes from the conventions and the Protocols, not from the resolution.

Cargo Ship Safety Construction, Cargo Ship Safety Equipment, Cargo Ship Safety Radio, IOPP and the other MARPOL certificates
Only the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment and Cargo Ship Safety Radio certificates
When
Each anniversary date, within three months either side
Equipment: at the second or third anniversary, replacing the annual survey that would otherwise fall there. Radio: at every anniversary date
What is done

blocks.p: The point most often got wrong: the radio periodical survey happens at every anniversary, so for the radio certificate the periodical survey replaces the annual rather than supplementing it. For safety equipment it falls once in the cycle, at the second or third anniversary.
The examiner asked for the relevance to the harmonized system, not only the difference, and this is where the second half of limb (b)'s marks are.

ul: A five-year certificate needs mid-cycle checkpoints to remain credible. Without them the Administration would be certifying for five years on the strength of one survey, which is not a safety judgement but an assumption.

Equipment is consumed in a way that structure is not. Lifejackets, liferafts, breathing apparatus, extinguishers, pyrotechnics and immersion suits degrade, expire and are used up - so they need a closer look partway through the cycle than a general annual examination provides.

Distress communication cannot be allowed to degrade unnoticed, which is why the radio survey is periodical at every anniversary rather than annual: the consequence of an undetected failure is that the ship cannot call for help at the moment she needs to.

The graded structure is the point. Annual, intermediate, periodical and renewal are a ladder of increasing depth matched to how quickly each thing can deteriorate - and matching survey effort to deterioration rate is what makes a five-year cycle safe rather than merely convenient.

Harmonisation makes the ladder practical. Common anniversary dates and the three-month window let all the surveys due at a given point be taken in one attendance, which is what stopped a ship being surveyed almost continuously by different attendances for different certificates - the problem the 1988 Protocols existed to solve.

blocks.p: Eight and eight on this paper, and that matters, because the same question at other sittings has been set at ten and six. Here the survey limb is worth exactly as much as the classification limb, so steps 6 to 8 must be developed rather than sketched. A candidate who writes a long essay on classification and finishes with four lines on surveys has thrown away a quarter of the question.

Within limb (a) the highest-value material is step 5 - why the SOLAS reference exists. Within limb (b) it is step 8 - the relevance, which the examiner asked for explicitly and which most candidates omit in favour of listing survey types.

The odd thing about SOLAS is what it does not contain. It has a great deal to say about stability, fire and life-saving, and nothing at all about how thick a plate has to be - hull strength was always the societies' private business with the owner and the underwriter. Regulation II-1/3-1 is SOLAS pointing at that private rule book and saying: that one, and you must keep to it for the ship's whole life. That is how losing class stopped being a commercial embarrassment and became a breach of the Convention.

Limb (b) is a different kind of question. Two survey names that sound interchangeable are not, and the reason they differ is that things deteriorate at different rates - so the depth of inspection is graded to match.

ul: Treating classification and statutory work as one function. They are separate, and only the second is delegated by the flag State.
Saying the flag State transfers its responsibility to the society. It transfers the work, not the duty.
Answering the SOLAS half of limb (a) by quoting the regulation without saying why it exists.
Missing the word maintained in II-1/3-1 - it is the word that makes class a continuing obligation.

Saying the periodical survey applies to all certificates. It applies only to safety equipment and safety radio.
Saying the radio periodical survey is once in the cycle. It is at every anniversary.
Answering limb (b) with a list of survey types and never reaching the relevance.
'Which certificates have a periodical survey?' Only Cargo Ship Safety Equipment and Cargo Ship Safety Radio.
'When is the equipment periodical survey?' At the second or third anniversary, replacing the annual that would otherwise fall there.
'How often is the radio periodical survey?' At every anniversary date.
'What is the survey window?' Three months either side of the anniversary date.
'Your ship loses class. Is that a SOLAS matter?' Yes - regulation II-1/3-1 requires the ship to be maintained in compliance with recognized class rules, so loss of class is a non-compliance.
'Must a ship be classed?' Not necessarily with a society - an Administration may apply national standards providing an equivalent level of safety.
'Which regulation recognizes the organization?' SOLAS XI-1/1, with the RO Code governing how it operates.
What is a condition of class? A requirement that a specified action be taken by a specified date, failing which class is suspended.
Name two alternatives to the standard machinery survey cycle. Continuous survey of machinery, and an approved planned maintenance scheme.
What did the 1988 Protocols actually change? They introduced the harmonized system - a common five-year cycle, common anniversary dates, the three-month window and combinable surveys.

Why does the association of classification societies publish unified requirements? To stop competitive rule differences between societies producing a race to the least demanding standard; member societies must incorporate them into their own rules.

How does II-1/3-1 relate to II-1/3-10? II-1/3-1 requires compliance with a recognized society's rules; II-1/3-10 goes further for bulk carriers and oil tankers of 150 m and above and requires those rules themselves to have been verified against goals set by IMO.

questions.understand_first: The odd thing about the great safety convention is what it does not contain. It has a great deal to say about stability, subdivision, fire protection and lifeboats, and nothing whatever about how thick a plate has to be or how big a shaft must be. Hull strength was never public law: it was a private arrangement between the owner, the underwriter and a society that had grown up to give an independent technical opinion on ships people were being asked to insure. That left an awkward gap - a ship could satisfy every word of the Convention and still be structurally substandard, and losing that private approval was a commercial embarrassment rather than a legal failure. The regulation in question closes the gap by pointing at the private rule book and giving it legal force, and the crucial word is that the ship must be not only designed and built to it but kept to it. The second half of the question is about something quite different: two survey names that sound interchangeable and are not. Things aboard a ship deteriorate at very different rates - steel slowly, lifejackets and pyrotechnics quickly, and a distress radio invisibly - so the depth of inspection is graded to match, and a certificate valid for five years is only honest if there are checkpoints in between.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish a classification society's two roles.
retrieval_cards.answer: Classification is private and contractual - it publishes rules and assigns and maintains class for the owner. Statutory work is different: where the flag State delegates survey and certification, the society acts as a recognized organization under SOLAS XI-1/1 and is governed by the RO Code. The Administration delegates the work but retains the responsibility.
retrieval_cards.why: The first discrimination on the question, and the SOLAS point in limb (a) is about the first role being given legal effect.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is compliance with class rules mentioned in SOLAS chapter II-1?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because SOLAS never contained scantling rules - hull strength was the societies' private business, so class was commercially indispensable but legally optional. Regulation II-1/3-1 requires ships to be designed, constructed AND MAINTAINED in compliance with the structural, mechanical and electrical requirements of a society recognized under regulation XI-1/1, or with national standards of equivalent safety. Because of the word 'maintained', loss of class became a SOLAS non-compliance, enforceable by the flag State and inspectable by port State control.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner asked why, not what - and 'maintained' is the word that carries the answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How are class rules actually made?
retrieval_cards.answer: From service experience and defect returns across the surveyed fleet; from casualty investigation feedback; from research and direct calculation including finite element analysis and fatigue assessment; through technical committees of owners, builders, makers and surveyors; and harmonised through the association of classification societies' unified requirements, unified interpretations and procedural requirements, with the Common Structural Rules for Bulk Carriers and Oil Tankers as the fully harmonised case.
retrieval_cards.why: Asserting that societies simply write rules earns little; the mechanism is what the limb asks for.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What did the harmonized system of survey and certification change?
retrieval_cards.answer: Introduced by the 1988 SOLAS and Load Lines Protocols and later extended to the MARPOL Annexes, it gave a common five-year certificate cycle, common anniversary dates across certificates, a survey window of three months either side of the due date, and the ability to combine surveys into a single attendance instead of a succession of separate visits.
retrieval_cards.why: It is what makes the graded survey ladder practical rather than merely logical.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which certificates carry a periodical survey, and when?
retrieval_cards.answer: Only the Cargo Ship Safety Equipment and the Cargo Ship Safety Radio certificates. The equipment periodical survey falls at the second or third anniversary, replacing the annual that would otherwise fall there. The radio periodical survey falls at EVERY anniversary date.
retrieval_cards.why: Using 'periodical' loosely, or making the radio survey once-per-cycle, is the classic error on this limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why does the difference between annual and periodical surveys matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because a five-year certificate needs mid-cycle checkpoints to remain credible. Equipment is consumed in a way that structure is not - lifejackets, liferafts, breathing apparatus, extinguishers and pyrotechnics degrade, expire and are used up - so it needs a closer look partway through than a general annual examination gives. Distress communication cannot be allowed to degrade unnoticed, which is why the radio survey is periodical at every anniversary. The graded ladder matches survey depth to deterioration rate.
retrieval_cards.why: The examiner asked for relevance, not only difference, and this is where half the limb's marks sit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Must a ship be classed with a classification society?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not necessarily. Regulation II-1/3-1 permits the alternative of applicable national standards of the Administration which provide an equivalent level of safety. What the regulation compels is a recognised technical standard, not membership of any particular society.
retrieval_cards.why: It shows you have read the regulation rather than remembered a summary of it.

blocks.h: 1. What FSA is, and its objectives

blocks.p: Formal Safety Assessment is a structured and systematic methodology aimed at enhancing maritime safety - including protection of life, health, the marine environment and property - by using risk analysis and cost-benefit assessment. It is set out in the Revised Guidelines for its use in the IMO rule-making process, MSC-MEPC.2/Circ.12/Rev.2.

Start by saying what kind of thing it is, because the whole answer follows from it: FSA is a tool for making RULES, not for running a ship. The Company's obligation under the ISM Code to assess risks to its ships and personnel and to establish safeguards is a different exercise, done by a different body, at a different scale. Confusing the two is the framing error on this question.
Its objectives are:

ul: to provide a rational and systematic process for assessing the risks associated with shipping activity, and for evaluating the costs and benefits of options for reducing those risks;
to provide a means of evaluating new regulations or of comparing existing with proposed regulations, so that safety and environmental benefit can be balanced against cost;
to assist in demonstrating to decision makers that a proposed measure delivers benefits in proportion to what it costs;
to support equitable and consistent regulatory change and to aid the reaching of consensus among Member States, by making the reasoning visible rather than assertive.

blocks.p: One honest qualification belongs here: the Guidelines do not claim that FSA is applied in all circumstances. It is a tool for the questions that need it, not a mandatory precondition for every amendment.

ul: Proactive, not reactive. It argues about a rule before the rule exists, instead of after a casualty. This is the single most important characteristic and belongs first.
Structured and systematic, so that two studies of the same problem can be compared and the reasoning followed.
Transparent, documented and auditable - every assumption, data source and judgement is recorded, because the output is meant to persuade a committee of States.
Generic rather than ship-specific. It is applied to a generic model of a ship type, system or operation, not to one vessel. That is what makes the result usable as a rule.
Proportionate in depth. The work is screened so effort goes where the risk is, rather than being applied uniformly.
Iterative. The steps are not a one-way corridor - findings at a later step send you back to an earlier one, and step 5 draws on all of them.
Explicitly cost-aware. Alone among safety methods in common use, it requires the cost of a proposed measure to be estimated and compared with the risk it removes.

blocks.h: 3. The process - and the step that is not one of the five

blocks.p: Before step 1, the decision makers define the problem: the ship type, system or operation to be studied, the scope and boundaries, the operating conditions, and the relevant regulations. This is preparatory and it is NOT one of the five steps. Calling it step 1 and pushing hazard identification to step 2 is the commonest structural error on this question.
Two definitions are needed before going further:

ul: a hazard is a potential to threaten human life, health, property or the environment;
risk is the combination of the frequency of an occurrence and the severity of its consequence.

blocks.p: The five steps are then:

rows: Hazard Identification
What could go wrong?
Risk Analysis
How likely is it, and how bad?
Risk Control Options
What could be done about it?
Cost Benefit Assessment
What would that cost, against what it saves?
Recommendations for decision-making
What should therefore be required?

blocks.p: Purpose: to produce a prioritised list of hazards and of the accident scenarios they lead to, specific to the problem defined.

ul: The creative element - a structured group review by a balanced team of people with practical experience: seagoing officers, designers, operators, surveyors and risk specialists, using techniques such as structured what-if and hazard and operability review. Its purpose is to find hazards that the data do not contain because they have not happened yet.

The analytical element - casualty and incident data, port State control and class defect records, published studies and previous FSA work. Its purpose is to make sure known hazards are not overlooked.
Both are necessary. Data alone will miss the novel hazard; imagination alone will miss the common one.
A coarse analysis of causes and consequences is carried out for each hazard, sufficient only to rank it.

Ranking on a risk matrix of frequency against severity, so that the small number of scenarios carrying most of the risk are carried into step 2 and the rest are screened out - which is where the proportionality characteristic is actually applied.
Output: a ranked list of hazards and scenarios, with the initiating events identified.

blocks.p: Purpose: a detailed investigation of the causes and consequences of the important scenarios carried forward from step 1, and the quantification of the risk.

ul: Causes and initiating events are modelled - typically by fault tree analysis, which works backwards from an undesired event to the combinations of failures that produce it.
Consequences are modelled - typically by event tree analysis, which works forwards from an initiating event through the success or failure of each barrier to the range of outcomes.
The risk contribution tree joins the two and shows which contributors dominate the total risk, which is what tells the study where control effort will actually pay.
Risk is expressed for each category the method protects - risk to people, to the environment and to property - because a measure that reduces one may not reduce another.
Expert judgement is used where data are absent, and is identified as such rather than disguised as measurement.
Uncertainty and sensitivity must be reported. A result that changes completely when one uncertain input is varied is a result that has to be presented with that caveat, and the Guidelines require it.
Output: the high-risk areas needing control, and the models against which any proposed measure can be tested.
A risk control measure acts on one element of risk. A risk control option is a combination of measures grouped so that it can be evaluated and, if adopted, implemented as one thing.

A measure can act on frequency - preventing the event - or on consequence - limiting the harm once it occurs. Recognising which a proposed measure does is essential, because they are not interchangeable.
Measures are engineering (design, redundancy, materials), operational (procedures, checklists, manning, training) or managerial (systems, audit, reporting).
Options are aimed at the dominant contributors found in step 2, and are grouped so that each can be costed.

blocks.p: This is the step the question names last and the one that distinguishes FSA from ordinary risk assessment.

ul: Define the base case - the risk level established in step 2, against which every option is measured.

Estimate the costs of each option over the whole life cycle - design, build, installation, operation, maintenance, training, survey and inspection, and any loss of earning capacity - not the purchase price alone.
Estimate the benefits - the reduction in risk the option delivers, expressed in the same terms as the base case: fatalities and injuries averted, pollution avoided, property preserved.

Identify the interested entities that bear the cost and those that receive the benefit. They are frequently not the same party, and saying so is a mark, because it is the real reason a technically sound measure can fail politically.

Express cost-effectiveness as cost per unit of risk reduction. The recognised indices are the gross cost of averting a fatality and the net cost of averting a fatality, the net figure taking account of the economic benefits the measure also produces.
The gross figure is considered first, with the net used where the economic benefits are real and demonstrable.
Rank and screen the options on that basis, so that the ones that buy the most risk reduction per unit of cost are carried into step 5.
There is no mandatory monetary criterion in the Guidelines. The indices support the argument; they do not decide it.

blocks.h: 8. Step 5 - Recommendations, and what FSA does not settle

ul: The recommendations must be auditable and traceable back through the four preceding steps, so that a committee can see how a conclusion was reached and challenge any link in it.
They must be understandable by non-specialists - the audience is a committee of Member States, not a risk-engineering conference.
They should identify the options that keep risk as low as reasonably practicable, with the reasoning for the practicability judgement stated.
They are submitted in a form the decision maker can act on: specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound.

blocks.p: And the honest limit, which is the closing judgement: FSA does not tell anyone how much risk is acceptable. There is no universally agreed acceptance criterion, and the Guidelines do not supply one. What the method does is force the criteria actually used to be stated explicitly, so that the judgement about tolerability is made openly by Member States rather than buried inside a calculation. That is a strength presented as a limitation, and saying so is the highest-value sentence available on this question.

Sixteen marks, no limbs, and the question names three of the five steps for 'specific explanation' - hazard identification, risk analysis and cost benefit assessment. Those three must be developed; the other two must still be present, because the question also asks for the processes as a whole and a three-step FSA is wrong.

The commonest failure is to spend the whole answer on the five steps and never address objectives and characteristics, which are two of the three things the stem asks for by name. Steps 1 and 2 of the route exist to stop that.

The point of the method is that it argues about a rule before the rule exists, instead of after a casualty. It forces the Organization to say what could go wrong, how likely and how bad it would be, what could be done about it, what that would cost - and only then what should be required. What it does not do, and says so plainly, is tell anyone how much risk is acceptable. That judgement stays with Member States; the method simply makes them state it out loud.

ul: Making problem definition step 1 and pushing hazard identification to step 2. Problem definition is preparatory and is not one of the five.
Confusing FSA with the risk assessment a company does under the ISM Code. Different body, different scale, different purpose.
Answering only the process and ignoring objectives and characteristics.
Treating the steps as strictly sequential. The method is iterative.
Giving hazard identification as a brainstorm only. It has a creative and an analytical element and needs both.
Costing only the purchase price of a measure. The assessment is over the whole life cycle.
Confusing a risk control measure with a risk control option.
Inventing an acceptance criterion. The Guidelines contain no mandatory monetary threshold.
'What is step 1?' Hazard identification. Problem definition comes before the five steps and is not one of them.
'Define risk.' The combination of the frequency of an occurrence and the severity of its consequence.
'Which tool for causes, which for consequences?' Fault tree backwards from the undesired event for causes; event tree forwards from the initiating event for consequences.
'What do GCAF and NCAF mean?' Gross and net cost of averting a fatality - cost per unit of risk reduction, with the net figure accounting for the economic benefits the measure also produces.
'Who pays and who benefits?' Frequently different parties - which is exactly why interested entities must be identified.
'How much risk is acceptable?' The method does not say. It requires the criterion used to be made explicit.
'Is FSA used for every amendment?' No - the Guidelines do not claim it is applied in all circumstances.

What is the difference between FSA and the risk assessment you do on board? FSA is a rule-making tool applied to a generic model of a ship type; onboard risk assessment applies to your ship, your plant and today's job under the safety management system.
Why is a generic model used rather than a real ship? Because the output has to support a rule that will apply to a class of ships, not a decision about one.
What is a risk contribution tree? The combination of the fault-tree and event-tree modelling that shows which contributors dominate the total risk.
Why must uncertainty be reported? Because a conclusion that reverses when one uncertain input is varied is not a safe basis for a regulation, and the committee has to know that.

Give an engineering, an operational and a managerial risk control measure for the same hazard. For engine-room fire: fixed extinguishing and hot-work-free design; hot-work permits and watchkeeping rounds; and a maintenance and audit regime for fuel-line insulation.

blocks.p: Objectives, characteristics, process - the three things the stem names, in that order. For the process: define the problem first, then HI, RA, RCO, CBA, REC. For each of the three named steps remember its question: what could go wrong, how likely and how bad, what would it cost. Close on the limit - FSA does not decide what is acceptable.

The method is therefore set out as established instrument content: nothing is presented as a verbatim quotation from a text that was not read, and no provision has been invented to give the answer authority it does not have. Two propositions that are easy to get wrong were settled deliberately rather than carried across from anywhere. The first is that defining the problem is not one of the five steps - it is what the decision makers do before the study starts, and treating it as step 1 misnumbers everything after it. The second is that the method does not decide how much risk is acceptable; it makes whatever criterion is being used visible, which is a different and more honest thing. The answer is also written about the method itself and uses no dated example study, which is deliberate: an example anchored to a particular programme of work would tie the answer to a moment, and this question has been set repeatedly over many years without the method changing.

questions.understand_first: The point of this method is that it argues about a rule before the rule exists, instead of after a casualty. Historically maritime regulation was written in the aftermath of disasters, which meant the price of every rule was paid before it was made. This is the attempt to do it the other way round: work out what could go wrong, how likely and how serious it would be, what could be done about it, what that would cost and who would pay - and only then decide what should be required. Two things about it are easy to miss. It is used to make rules for a whole class of ships, so it is applied to a representative model rather than to any real vessel, which is quite different from the risk assessment a chief engineer signs before a job. And it deliberately stops short of the last question. It will tell a committee how much a proposed measure costs for each life it would save; it will not tell them whether that price is worth paying. That judgement belongs to the member States, and the method's real contribution is to force them to say out loud what standard they are applying rather than leaving it buried inside a calculation.
